Rejects medical intervention preemptively, explicitly stating 'I don't want any medication' when a doctor is suggested.

ambivalence.for_change: The client expresses a desire to not 'feel like this anymore' and is 'willing to at least give it a go' by talking to someone.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The client fears that accepting help, especially medical, would mean admitting to a chemical or inherent flaw that contradicts their self-view of the problem as having no clear cause.

values_and_stakes: The autonomy and self-reliance implied by not being a 'bother' to friends and family.
The identity of being someone who does not rely on pharmaceutical intervention ('I don't want to take any pills or anything like that').
(inferred) The perceived stability of their current state, which, while painful, is familiar and doesn't require confronting an unknown cause or treatment path.
key_facts: The client has not spoken to friends, family, or a doctor about their depression prior to this session.
The client has identified their sister as the first person they will speak to about their feelings.
The client's depressive symptoms have been worsening over time, not staying static.

background: (inferred) A married person without a job, living paycheck to paycheck with a husband who pays all the bills.
self_view_of_problem: I overspent on Christmas gifts I couldn't return, and now I feel guilty and overwhelmed because I have no idea how to pay my credit cards off.
resistance_drivers: Rejects practical suggestions by immediately restating the core constraint ('I have no job') as a block to any action.
Corrects the therapist's role assumption to maintain the frame of receiving help as a stranger, not as a fellow worker.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I feel guilty and overwhelmed by the debt and want to find a way to pay it off.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Admitting full responsibility and changing spending behavior threatens my self-image and could confirm my husband's blame.

values_and_stakes: Financial security within the marriage, as the husband pays all bills and they live paycheck to paycheck.
The marital relationship, as the husband has already blamed her for the spending.
(inferred) Personal autonomy and the ability to make purchases without causing a crisis.
key_facts: The client has a minimum credit card payment of $100 due in a week.
The client purchased items online on sale with a no-return policy.
The client's husband handles all household bills and subscriptions.

background: (inferred) A person in a two-year romantic relationship, with a social circle of friends who are aware of their feelings.
self_view_of_problem: I need to break up with my girlfriend because my feelings have changed, and I don't know how to handle it without hurting her.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by asking for procedural specifics when therapist suggests action (e.g., 'I'm not sure what you mean by the right time. Is there ever a right time?')
Expresses worry and fear about the partner's potential negative reaction as a reason for inaction

ambivalence.for_change: I think it might be easier to stay together but I don't think that's the right thing to do.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear of causing emotional distress to someone he cares about and of losing the relationship's positive history.

values_and_stakes: The current friendship and goodwill with his girlfriend
His self-image as a caring person who avoids hurting others
(inferred) The stability and comfort of the existing relationship structure
key_facts: He has felt his feelings have changed for a while and is thinking about it more now.
He has friends who know how he is feeling and who he might ask for help.
He acknowledges the therapist's suggestion to be honest and have the conversation.

background: (inferred) A person living paycheck to paycheck with significant credit card debt, who recently signed up for a credit card a year ago.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is needing to come up with $100 by next week to meet the minimum charge on a credit card to avoid a 24% interest penalty, which is causing a panic attack.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from exploring systemic or emotional causes by immediately focusing on practical solutions (e.g., shifts from therapist's question about company responsibility to the idea of a balance transfer).
(inferred) Avoids examining personal spending patterns or underlying financial habits when presented with an opportunity to do so.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) Wants to relieve the immediate anxiety and pressure of the looming payment deadline.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Is attached to the short-term relief and perceived benefits of spending (e.g., 'there was such a great deal'), which conflicts with long-term financial stability.

values_and_stakes: Financial stability and avoiding punitive interest rates (the 24% penalty).
(inferred) Maintaining self-reliance and not burdening friends or family who are also financially strained.
(inferred) Preserving the ability to access 'great deals' and the immediate gratification they provide.
key_facts: The client is currently experiencing a panic attack due to the financial deadline.
The client has not contacted the credit card company to explain their situation.
The client signed up for the credit card knowing the terms a year ago.

background: (inferred) The client is employed in an office workplace with colleagues who hold anti-mask views, and has personally lost people to the COVID-19 pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is that my co-workers believe the pandemic is a government conspiracy, which is hurtful and scary because the pandemic is real and puts everyone's health at risk in the workplace.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from personal anxiety to others' flawed reasoning when therapist suggests calming techniques.
Deflects by questioning the therapist's viewpoint when feeling the core conflict is not being addressed.

ambivalence.for_change: I want the anxiety to stop and to feel safe and respected at work.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A pull away from fully asserting my needs stems from a fear of disrupting workplace harmony or being seen as disrespectful to colleagues' positions.

values_and_stakes: Respectful co-working relationships with colleagues whose life positions I acknowledge.
My physical health and safety from COVID-19 and other illnesses in the shared workplace.
The psychological safety and reduced anxiety for myself and others at work.
key_facts: The client has lost people to COVID-19, which makes co-workers' conspiracy views personally hurtful.
The client's manager is scheduled to review workplace guidelines with the team on Monday.
The client uses breathing exercises in the moment to manage anxiety, as they did while typing during the session.

background: (inferred) A person with a close friend group, living under lockdown conditions that have disrupted normal face-to-face social contact.
self_view_of_problem: I am worried about a friend who has become quiet and non-responsive since lockdown, and I want to make sure they are okay.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from personal action to external validation by immediately asking the therapist for a solution ('Now what should I do about them?')
Expresses uncertainty and lack of closeness as a barrier to following a concrete suggestion (e.g., contacting family).
(inferred) Minimizes own concern by readily accepting alternative, less worrying explanations for the friend's behavior.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to make sure my friend is okay and feel a responsibility to act because other friends are also concerned.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear of overstepping boundaries or being seen as intrusive if I take direct action to investigate my friend's situation.

values_and_stakes: The specific friendship with the non-responsive individual, which is at risk of fading.
Their role and standing within the broader peer group that is collectively concerned.
(inferred) Their self-image as a caring but not overbearing or intrusive person.
key_facts: The client has not attempted to contact the friend's family.
Other friends in the peer group share the client's concern.
The friend is typically outgoing, making their current quietness seem odd.

background: A person currently employed but at risk of layoff, the sole income earner in their family after their wife was laid off earlier this year, and they are dipping into savings to afford their home.
self_view_of_problem: I'm worried I'm going to be in the next round of layoffs at my company, and if I'm laid off, we can't afford our home.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions by citing prior failed efforts (e.g., when therapist suggests job search methods, client states they've already tried and faced obstacles).
Expresses hopelessness and frustration when offered optimistic reframing, reinforcing a sense of being stuck.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to find a new job or secure my current one to provide for my family and stop dipping into savings.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I am attached to the security and identity of my current job and fear the unknown of a job search that feels futile.

values_and_stakes: Financial stability and ability to afford our home.
My role as the sole provider for my family.
(inferred) My professional identity and sense of competence in my career.
key_facts: My company just laid off 10% of the workforce and furloughed another 10%.
I've sent out 50 resumes and got 3 interviews in the past month.
My wife was laid off earlier this year, and we are already dipping into savings.

background: (inferred) A working professional with a partner and childcare responsibilities, currently employed and applying for a new corporate job.
self_view_of_problem: I have an interview in 3 days and I'm getting really nervous because I think I need longer to prepare, especially since it's a corporate interview requiring behavioral answers that usually take me a week to learn.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by asking the therapist for personal anecdotes when feeling stressed about time pressure.
Immediately counters potential solutions with practical obstacles (e.g., short notice for leave, busy at work).

ambivalence.for_change: I think I need to stay positive and aim for confidence, and I should try to relax and just give it my best shot instead of perfection.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear that acting differently (e.g., preparing less thoroughly) will increase nervousness and reduce interview performance.

values_and_stakes: Current job performance and professional reputation (concerned about taking short-notice leave or finishing early).
Relationship with partner (considering asking them to take on extra childcare).
Chances of getting the new job (worried delaying the interview might affect opportunities).
key_facts: The interview is in 3 days and requires behavioral answers the client normally takes a week to prepare.
The client is very busy at work and sees taking leave on short notice as difficult.
The client has a partner and childcare responsibilities that could be rearranged.

background: (inferred) A person involved in a board or organizational activity, who has a history of dating and complicated social dynamics with a man who leads that board.
self_view_of_problem: I'm confused about whether he has feelings for me and what his motives are for asking me to work on the board with him, and it's a twisted situation.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by focusing on external benefits (like board perks and clout) when therapist suggests a clean break or labels behavior as manipulative.
Uses passive, time-dependent reasoning ('I'll know sooner or later,' 'it will become clearer in time') to avoid taking decisive action or direct confrontation.
Justifies continued involvement by framing it as mutually beneficial ('he is encouraging me to be like that. cuz it helps him too') when therapist points out manipulation.

ambivalence.for_change: I think I would be better being away from the situation, and I don't think it's a healthy relationship.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear of losing the social advantage, validation, and connection that the board position and his attention provide, especially when other options feel limited.

values_and_stakes: Her position and perks on the board, which give her 'an upper edge and more clout'.
The potential for rekindling a romantic relationship with him, which she is still wondering about.
(inferred) Her social standing and power dynamics within the friend/board circle, which could be disrupted by a clean break.
key_facts: She slept with one of his friends and another friend wanted to sleep with her, which he suspected.
She agreed to work with him on the board when he asked, citing that he said he trusts her.
She tried to break away once before, but 'they asked me to come back'.

background: (inferred) A working adult with credit card debt, likely employed but needing more hours or a second job to manage finances.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is a credit card interest rate increase that requires working more hours to pay off the debt faster, though they acknowledge they will pay it off within 2-3 years and dislike the waiting.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from practical financial planning by shifting to external topics (e.g., weather, student loan forgiveness).
Expresses reluctance to cut discretionary spending, framing it as feeling deprived if they go 'too much' into that money.

ambivalence.for_change: They want to pay off the debt sooner to reduce interest and not wait 2-3 years.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) They are attached to the immediate gratification and pleasure of discretionary spending on items like chocolate and nice things.

values_and_stakes: Maintaining discretionary spending on personal treats and 'nice things'.
Avoiding feelings of deprivation from overly strict budgeting.
key_facts: Their no-interest credit card period expired, triggering an $80 monthly interest increase.
They anticipate paying off the debt in 2-3 years, with a preference for closer to two years.
They have a history of spending discretionary money on themselves, like chocolate, rather than allocating it to debt.

background: (inferred) A person with a close friend who is dating a drug addict, and who has prior family experience with addiction (alcoholism).
self_view_of_problem: I am confused and sad about having to distance myself from a long-time friend because she is dating a drug addict and thief, which puts me at risk and forces me to watch her potentially destroy her life.
resistance_drivers: Seeks external validation for their decision when feeling uncertain (e.g., asks 'Am I wrong?').
Deflects from fully committing to therapist suggestions by citing conflicting family opinions ('they don't think it's that big of a deal').

ambivalence.for_change: I feel confident I need to distance myself to stay safe and healthy, and I recognize enabling doesn't help.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I fear the sadness and loss of ending a long-term friendship that has been a significant part of my life.

values_and_stakes: The long-term friendship itself, which is at risk of being lost.
Personal financial and emotional safety, which is threatened by the boyfriend's borrowing and stealing.
(inferred) The role of being a supportive, caring person, which conflicts with the need to set boundaries.
key_facts: The friend's boyfriend has borrowed money from the client and others multiple times and has stolen from people.
The client has had family members who were alcoholics and previously bailed them out until realizing it made no difference.
The client's family does not think the current situation with the friend is a big deal.

background: (inferred) A student on the East Coast, living in an apartment, with courses finishing by the end of December.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is external: a pandemic causing fear, anxiety, and anger at others' foolishness, combined with internal struggles of procrastination, lack of structure, and needing more discipline and time-management.
resistance_drivers: Externalizes blame onto others (e.g., 'youth groups,' apartment neighbors) when discussing distress, deflecting from deeper personal accountability.
Uses intellectualized agreement and future-oriented planning ('revamp my style in the new year') to avoid engaging with present emotional difficulties or implementing immediate changes.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) They desire to feel more in control, less emotionally affected, and to improve their discipline and time-management to reduce stress.
ambivalence.against_change: They are attached to a self-image of moral superiority and control ('not compromise my values') that is reinforced by judging others, which might be threatened by examining their own contributions to their stress.

values_and_stakes: Their sense of moral integrity and doing what is 'right' during the pandemic, which is tied to their identity.
Their academic performance and successful completion of courses by December.
(inferred) Their autonomy and self-reliance, as they emphasize overcoming impatience and fatigue on their own.
key_facts: They procrastinate a lot, leading to falling behind on academic work and missing workouts.
Their courses are nearly finished by the end of December, after which they plan to 'revamp' their style.
They live in an apartment where they observe neighbors going out frequently, which angers them.

background: (inferred) A person experiencing social isolation, likely during the COVID-19 pandemic, with friends who have differing views on safety.
self_view_of_problem: I can't connect with friends much anymore because they want to meet in person and I just can't, and I don't think they take COVID seriously.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by asking for therapist suggestions when faced with the difficulty of direct communication.
Expresses helplessness ('I just can't') when confronted with the core action required to bridge the gap.

ambivalence.for_change: I miss my friends so much and want to find a way to show I care.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear of compromising personal safety or values regarding COVID-19, which feels non-negotiable.

values_and_stakes: The specific friendships she currently has and misses.
Her sense of personal safety and adherence to her COVID-19 precautions.
(inferred) Her identity as a caring friend who makes efforts.
key_facts: She has already tried calling her friends but it did not resolve the impasse.
She identifies that one friend is more receptive to a third party (another friend) than to her directly.
She responds positively to the therapist's anecdote about cards, indicating openness to indirect, non-physical gestures.

background: (inferred) A homeowner who has lived in their current house for almost ten years, likely living alone or with family given the focus on household disarray and shame about visitors.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as feeling ashamed because their house is 'so disorganized' and 'every single room is disarrayed,' to the point they won't let anyone come over.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus or disengages when asked about the origin or causes of the problem (e.g., apologizes, asks if the therapist is still there after being asked 'When did this begin?' and 'What do you feel like brought you into this situation?').
Expresses a resigned, passive stance that minimizes the problem's urgency (e.g., states 'What is sad is now I really don’t care anymore').

ambivalence.for_change: The client wants to 'feel less ashamed' and has a desire for social connection, as indicated by their distress over not letting anyone come over.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A protective emotional pull toward maintaining the current state to avoid the overwhelming effort and potential failure of tackling a decade-long accumulation of disorganization.

values_and_stakes: Social connection and hospitality — the ability to have guests over without shame.
Self-respect and a sense of order — living in a home that feels organized and cared for.
(inferred) Personal identity as a competent, capable homeowner — at risk of being undermined by the chronic disarray.
key_facts: The problem began about ten years ago, shortly after moving into the house and getting settled.
The client states they 'really don’t care anymore,' indicating a current state of resignation.
The disorganization is severe enough that the client actively prevents anyone from visiting.

background: (inferred) A person with at least one close friendship, navigating interpersonal conflict.
self_view_of_problem: I have a friend who is not listening to me, not accepting how I feel, and is being very dismissive and rude.
resistance_drivers: Shifts from accepting therapist's reframe to reasserting the friend's negative behavior and own reluctance to engage.
Seeks concrete action steps but expresses doubt about their efficacy given the perceived severity of the friend's rudeness.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to resolve the conflict and have a plan to reach out, because I value the friendship and feel less upset with a path forward.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I am attached to my feeling of being wronged and my right to be angry, which makes me reluctant to initiate contact.

values_and_stakes: The specific friendship with this person, which is normally good.
My sense of being heard and respected within that friendship.
key_facts: The client states the friend's dismissive behavior is a recent deviation from her normally good listening.
The client acknowledges she can also need space when things are bad.
The client plans to give time for both parties to calm down before potentially reaching out.

background: (inferred) A person with a social circle of friends who want to gather in person, living in an area with COVID-19 government restrictions on gatherings.
self_view_of_problem: I can't figure out why my friends don't understand why I want to keep a bit distant during COVID.
resistance_drivers: Expresses skepticism about the adequacy of virtual alternatives (e.g., questioning how connection is possible over Skype).
Focuses on the perceived loss or difficulty of the new method (e.g., highlighting the lack of physical contact) rather than its potential.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to maintain my friendships and please my friends.
ambivalence.against_change: I feel a pull away from change because virtual connection feels like an inadequate substitute for the physical contact and in-person activities I value.

values_and_stakes: The physical, in-person connection with friends.
The ability to participate in shared, in-person activities with friends.
Friends' understanding and approval of my cautious stance.
key_facts: The client's friends want to gather in person despite government orders limiting gatherings.
The client does not drink alcohol.
The client found the therapist's 'absence makes the heart grow fonder' framing to be a positive new perspective.

background: Works in the live event industry (concert audio) with a side hustle in carpentry, currently unemployed since March due to COVID-19 shutdowns, lives with housemates who don't drive, and has asthma and a blood disorder that compromises their immune system.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is being out of work with a stalled unemployment system, surviving on insufficient DoorDash income, and worrying about their car breaking down while feeling underqualified for remote jobs.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Deflects from deeper emotional distress by focusing on practical obstacles (e.g., car condition, job qualifications) when discussing solutions.
(inferred) Minimizes their own agency by attributing lack of progress to external factors (unemployment system, employer disinterest) rather than exploring internal barriers.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) They desire financial stability and a safe, sustainable work-from-home job to reduce stress and protect their health.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) They are attached to their identity and skills in concert audio and carpentry, fearing that shifting to unfamiliar remote work threatens their professional self-worth.

values_and_stakes: Their health and safety (due to asthma and a blood disorder) is at risk if they take unsafe work.
Their car, which is essential for current income (DoorDash), is at risk of breaking down from overuse.
Their professional identity and skills in concert audio and carpentry are at risk if they abandon their field for generic remote work.
key_facts: They have been applying only for work-from-home jobs due to health vulnerabilities.
They drive an old car that limits their DoorDash hours to daylight only.
They feel underqualified for the remote jobs they are applying for.

background: (inferred) A working adult, likely in their late 20s or 30s, who lives independently and has a close relationship with their mother and brother.
self_view_of_problem: I am very sad and more depressed than ever because I recently broke up with my girlfriend after spending the last few years with her, including a lot of time together during quarantine.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from emotional processing to practical, future-oriented questions (e.g., asking for advice on timelines for dating) when the therapist validates or explores feelings.
(inferred) Minimizes the depth of his sadness by emphasizing planned distractions (going out, exercise) rather than exploring the grief.

ambivalence.for_change: He acknowledges feeling depressed and seeks support from family and therapy, indicating a desire to feel better.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is attached to the identity and timeline of being the oldest sibling who should already have a family, making full grieving feel like falling further behind.

values_and_stakes: His role and status as the oldest sibling in his family, compared to his married younger brother and sister.
The long-term, intimate partnership he had with his girlfriend, built over years and intensified during quarantine.
His privacy and boundary between personal life and coworkers, which limits his support network at work.
key_facts: He is going out tonight to meet friends for happy hour to take his mind off things.
He has gone for long runs and swims as a coping activity.
He has been talking to his mother and brother about the breakup and finds it helpful.

background: (inferred) A woman in Pennsylvania, married, with a long-term diagnosis of major clinical depression, currently not in treatment.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as an ongoing, treatment-resistant depression that makes her tired all the time and unable to get out of bed, and as being under her husband's control, which she describes as 'a long story'.
resistance_drivers: Deflects or shuts down conversation by stating the problem is too big or long-term for the current interaction (e.g., 'It's more than one 15 min conversation can do').
Uses passive resignation or withdrawal (e.g., stating she's going to lay down) when the therapist suggests actionable steps or challenges her situation.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) She acknowledges the therapist is right about her controlling relationship being an issue, indicating some internal recognition that her situation is not okay.
ambivalence.against_change: She feels a pull away from change due to a long-standing attachment to a sense of helplessness and a belief that past treatments (over 20 medicines, therapy years ago) have definitively failed.

values_and_stakes: (inferred) Her marital relationship and the stability of her current home life are at risk if she challenges her husband's control.
(inferred) Her established identity as someone with an intractable, long-term condition is at risk if she pursues new treatment and it might work.
key_facts: She has been diagnosed with major clinical depression over 20 years ago.
She has tried over 20 medicines and therapy years ago, and states 'nothing helped'.
She states her husband doesn't allow her to seek therapy and that he 'got me under his control'.

background: (inferred) A student in a high-stakes, expensive academic program, likely in college or a professional certification course, facing significant financial pressure from tuition costs.
self_view_of_problem: I'm driving myself crazy worrying about school, and I can't sleep at night worrying about my upcoming test because it's so much pressure to succeed and the classes are so expensive.
resistance_drivers: Immediately cites external constraints (COVID-19) when a solution (study groups) is suggested, shutting down the initial idea.
(inferred) Catastrophizes financial outcomes (debt with nothing to show) when discussing failure, which amplifies anxiety and blocks problem-solving.

ambivalence.for_change: I sure do want to come up with a plan to move forward and feel better.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear that any action (like trying a new study method) won't be enough to prevent the catastrophic financial and academic failure I'm imagining.

values_and_stakes: Financial stability and avoiding crippling debt from having to retake an expensive class.
Academic success and obtaining a degree to validate the investment and effort.
(inferred) Personal competence and self-worth, tied to passing this high-stakes test.
key_facts: The client is currently unable to sleep due to test anxiety.
The client has already identified and rejected in-person study groups as an option due to COVID-19.
The client responded positively to the therapist's personal anecdote about overcoming a repeated class.

background: A parent with three children, previously worked in a deli in the food industry before being laid off due to COVID-19, now relies on internet-based gig work like Amazon MTurk for income.
self_view_of_problem: I can't find a career and I'm stressed; I don't know where to look for work, don't trust it's safe to work, and feel anxious most of the time thinking about it.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus to practical tools or immediate tasks when therapist probes about broader career planning or emotional fears (e.g., asks about Chrome extensions instead of addressing anxiety about work safety).
Expresses gratitude and agreement quickly, potentially to avoid deeper exploration of underlying stress or helplessness (e.g., 'thankyou', 'that sounds helpful').

ambivalence.for_change: I need guidance and am interested in ways to use my computer to make money because I have three kids and Christmas is coming, which is good motivation.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Changing to a traditional or new field of work feels threatening due to fear of COVID-19 safety risks and anxiety about the unknown.

values_and_stakes: Providing for three children, especially with Christmas approaching.
Maintaining the ability to work from home for perceived safety and flexibility.
Preserving the motivation and instant payment structure from gig work that helps manage financial stress.
key_facts: The client made almost $300 in a month using Amazon MTurk but says it's not quite enough yet.
The client's unemployment benefits have run out and they are unsure how to reapply.
The client has only worked in the food industry and is unsure what other field to look into.

background: He is an army veteran who has returned to the country, has an 8-year-old daughter and five-year-old twin boys, and is concerned about protecting his family and home.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as a threat to his ability to protect his children and home due to potential gun policy changes and unreliable police response, stating 'i want to protect my children from harm' and 'i feel we have to take it upon ourselves.'
resistance_drivers: Dismisses alternatives when the therapist suggests exploring them, using sarcasm ('what should i do...throw a knife at them? lol') to shut down the discussion.
Minimizes his own worry after the therapist validates his protective stance, deflecting from deeper exploration ('true..i may be worrying over nothing').
(inferred) Resists discussing emotional coping practices due to embarrassment, as seen when he calls journaling and meditation 'kinda embarasing to admit...'

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) He feels a pull to manage his worry more effectively, as evidenced by his engagement with VA-recommended practices like journaling and deep breathing, though he finds them embarrassing.
ambivalence.against_change: He is emotionally attached to his identity as a protector who relies on personal firearm ownership, seeing any change as a threat to his ability to safeguard his family.

values_and_stakes: His role as the primary protector of his children and home.
His identity and practical competence as an army veteran who defended the country.
(inferred) His sense of autonomy and self-reliance in a system he perceives as unreliable.
key_facts: He cites a specific incident where police took 35 minutes to respond to his neighbor's domestic violence call.
He has three young children: an 8-year-old daughter and five-year-old twin boys.
The VA has him practicing journaling, deep breathing, and meditation for worry management.

background: (inferred) A young adult living with a roommate, likely in an urban or shared living situation, with a close-knit family and social connections.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as a sudden, unexplained wave of grief over their grandmother's death, compounded by frustration at their roommate's lack of consideration and their own feeling of being trapped in their room.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from deeper emotional exploration by shifting focus to external frustrations, like the roommate's behavior.
Uses minimization and future-oriented optimism ('it will be over sooner than later') to avoid sitting with the intensity of present grief.
(inferred) Resists suggestions for new coping strategies (like online groups or virtual meetups) by affirming they already have coping methods ('I can usually cope with the loss fairly well').

ambivalence.for_change: They acknowledge the grief is overwhelming today and wish they weren't stuck in their room, indicating a desire for relief from the sadness and isolation.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Holding onto the grief feels like a way to maintain a connection to their grandmother, who was their primary emotional support, so letting go might feel like losing that link.

values_and_stakes: The deep, irreplaceable relationship with their grandmother as their primary confidante and source of comfort.
Their need for personal space and autonomy in their shared living environment.
(inferred) Their self-image as someone who is usually competent at coping with loss, which would be challenged if they fully embraced their current vulnerability.
key_facts: Their grandmother died in September, and today is the first time in weeks they've felt this intense wave of grief.
They explicitly told their roommate they wanted to be alone today, but the roommate is having people over anyway.
They have seen family and friends occasionally recently, maintaining some social connection.

background: (inferred) A person with a close friend of five years, currently in a conflict over a perceived romantic entanglement.
self_view_of_problem: He sees the problem as a misunderstanding where his friend misjudged him, thinking he had an affair with the friend's girlfriend, which is a sensitive issue.
resistance_drivers: Shows passive acceptance of the friend's avoidance (blocking, ignoring) without proposing alternative actions to reconnect.
Seeks external direction ('please give me some suggestion') rather than generating his own solutions, indicating a reliance on being told what to do.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) He wants to resolve the conflict and restore the friendship because it is causing him sadness.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He fears that initiating a direct conversation about the affair accusation will be difficult and could worsen the sensitive situation.

values_and_stakes: A five-year friendship that is currently blocked and ignored.
(inferred) His social identity as a trustworthy person within his friend group.
key_facts: His friend has blocked him and is not responding to attempts at communication.
The conflict stems from the friend's belief he had an affair with the friend's girlfriend.
He reports feeling sad about the situation but better after talking to the therapist.

background: She is a single mother with a teenage son who is doing school from home. She is currently unemployed and struggling financially.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as being 'left behind' and 'floundering' without a clue what to do next, feeling like she is in a pit she'll never get out of because her identity as a mom is shifting as her son becomes more independent.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from exploring her own identity by immediately refocusing on her son's needs and her role as a mother.
Uses self-isolation and the pandemic as a reason to avoid social connection and new activities, even when they are suggested.

ambivalence.for_change: She admits she feels stuck and wants a path forward, and she agrees to try writing letters as a step.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is emotionally attached to her identity as a self-sacrificing mother, which provides a familiar role and excuses her from focusing on herself.

values_and_stakes: Her relationship with her teenage son, whom she describes as her best friend.
Her role and identity as a dedicated, always-available mother.
(inferred) Her sense of safety and reduced anxiety provided by her current isolated routine.
key_facts: She has been depressed for a really long time and no longer finds joy in things she used to like.
She has isolated herself and used the pandemic to ease her anxiety, making her life lonely.
She used to be active in online support groups for single parents but stopped because life 'got in the way'.

background: A 76-year-old retired woman, married, with an adult son in Florida who is currently unemployed and struggling financially. (inferred) She and her husband had planned to travel extensively during retirement.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as being trapped and unable to enjoy the rest of her life with her husband due to pandemic restrictions, compounded by grief from a friend's death and worry over her son's suffering.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions (like volunteering or teaching online) by immediately citing an external obstacle (virus risk, son's suffering).
Uses global, fatalistic statements ('there is nothing to do') when faced with the prospect of a long wait for improvement.

ambivalence.for_change: She wants to find ways to avoid getting 'too down and depressed' and acknowledges the need to try.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Changing her stance would feel like abandoning her identity as a caring mother who shouldn't enjoy life while her son suffers.

values_and_stakes: The ability to travel and enjoy active retirement years with her husband.
Her role and emotional connection as a supportive mother to her struggling son.
(inferred) Her sense of personal safety and health, which prevents a return to valued activities like nursing home volunteering.
key_facts: She is 76 years old and perceives a year of restrictions as a significant portion of her remaining time.
Her son in Florida lost his job and she feels she may need to provide financial help.
She previously volunteered at a nursing home but is now afraid to do so because of the virus.

background: A student taking two online courses, living alone and self-isolating since March due to the pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: Defines the problem as daily stresses from the pandemic disrupting routines, causing anxiety about the second wave, and leading to unproductive energy, lethargy, and disappointment in their own work ethics and health habits.
resistance_drivers: Dismisses external solutions (like contacting city officials) as ineffective or too slow, redirecting focus back to personal coping.
Agrees with therapist suggestions superficially ('good idea', 'match my thinking exactly') without committing to deeper exploration or change.
(inferred) Minimizes the severity of their own behavioral lapses (poor sleep, low motivation) by quickly pivoting to actions already taken (reducing phone use).

ambivalence.for_change: Admits feeling disappointed in their lapses in school work, sleep, and exercise, and wants to channel productive energy to finish deadlines.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Feels an attachment to the comfort and routine of isolation, having 'gotten used to it and more comfortable,' which makes engaging with external routines or changes threatening.

values_and_stakes: Academic performance and completion of two online courses ending this month and next.
Personal health routines (workout patterns, sleep patterns, diet) that have deteriorated.
(inferred) A sense of self-reliance and control over their environment, which would be challenged by relying on external authorities or drastic changes.
key_facts: The client only leaves home once or twice a week for work and once every two weeks for groceries.
They have been self-isolated since March and report feeling more comfortable with it now, though fear is returning.
They are in a 'crunch period' with school deadlines ending at the end of this month and next.

background: A woman who was in a ten-year relationship, works full-time, and was financially supporting herself and her boyfriend before the breakup.
self_view_of_problem: She frames it as a shocking, cruel breakup where her boyfriend left without discussion after losing his job, and she is mad about how he went about it, not necessarily missing him.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from deeper emotional pain by focusing on practical solutions or humor (e.g., getting a cat, joking about being a cat lady).
Minimizes the loss of the relationship by framing it as 'ten years gone down the drain' and 'that's life', avoiding prolonged grief.

ambivalence.for_change: She explicitly states she doesn't think she wants him back because he treated the relationship as a pawn.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is scared of being alone after ten years of cohabitation and fears missing the company more than the relationship itself.

values_and_stakes: Her sense of stability and companionship from living with a partner for ten years.
Her pride and self-respect after sticking her neck out for him against her parents' disapproval.
(inferred) Her established daily routine and shared home environment that provided comfort and predictability.
key_facts: She threw her phone in anger when he tried to contact her, breaking her means of communication.
She was the sole financial supporter for both herself and her boyfriend before the breakup.
She came home from work to find him packing without any prior discussion.

background: (inferred) A person experiencing significant social and cognitive difficulties, likely a student or young adult given the context of answering questions in front of others and the mention of partying.
self_view_of_problem: I am always in the mood of depression. I think the negative part only of everything I want to do, and I see myself as an example of uselessness.
resistance_drivers: Rejects simplistic, action-oriented advice by immediately presenting a counter-example or a deeper problem (e.g., when told to go out, states he has no girl friends; when told to change his mind, says he has tried and can't).
Responds to encouragement with self-deprecating absolutism that shuts down dialogue (e.g., when told not to feel useless, declares 'I am an example of Useless').

ambivalence.for_change: He explicitly asks for solutions to get out of his negative point of view, indicating a desire for relief.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A deep-seated attachment to a negative self-identity ('an example of Useless') that feels more true and safe than the uncertainty of change.

values_and_stakes: (inferred) Social competence and the ability to perform basic cognitive tasks (like answering questions or understanding language) without shame.
(inferred) A sense of personal agency and effectiveness, as his repeated failed attempts to 'change his mind' threaten his belief in his own capability.
key_facts: He states he has tried to change his mind many times but cannot.
He reports being unable to answer questions in front of others even when he knows the answer.
He claims he is not able to understand his mother tongue.

background: (inferred) An adult living in the U.S. during the pandemic, likely working or studying from home, given the context of discussing routines and societal anxiety.
self_view_of_problem: I am feeling very depressed lately, like a constant pressure that I don't know exactly what it is, and the days getting shorter makes it worse.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from personal action by shifting focus to existential or societal problems (e.g., mortality, government incompetence) when practical tips are offered.
Uses fatalistic or poetic statements ('Time is the fire in which we burn') to frame inertia as an intractable condition rather than a choice.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to overcome feeling depressed and find ways to enjoy mornings and have a better routine.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Changing my routine feels daunting because getting up is dreaded, creating a 'bad cycle' that feels hard to break.

values_and_stakes: (inferred) The comfort of familiar, albeit negative, cycles (like staying up late and dawning mornings) that define my current identity and daily rhythm.
A sense of intellectual or philosophical alignment found in contemplating existential insignificance, which might be disrupted by simplistic, action-oriented change.
key_facts: The client explicitly asks for tips on how to overcome depression.
The client acknowledges a 'bad cycle' of staying up late and dreading getting up.
The client finds comfort in the thought of cosmic insignificance ('a strangely comforting thought').

background: (inferred) A person going through a breakup, likely an adult with a partner and a sister who has been through a similar situation.
self_view_of_problem: I'm really anxious over a breakup and I don't know how to be alone or what to do.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Expresses helplessness and seeks external direction when faced with uncertainty about the future.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to feel better and less anxious about the breakup.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear of the loneliness and lack of direction that comes with being alone.

values_and_stakes: (inferred) The relationship with their partner, which is ending.
(inferred) Their sense of security and ability to function independently.
(inferred) Their emotional well-being and stability.
key_facts: The client is breaking up with their partner tomorrow.
The client states 'I don't know how to be alone.'
The client's sister has been through a similar situation.

background: A student juggling multiple academic deadlines (final exam, assignments) across at least two courses while also working a part-time job, and who has been in a pattern of late-night studying and disrupted routines since the pandemic began.
self_view_of_problem: Frames the problem as a 'pattern' of procrastination, distraction, and bad habits (sleep, eating, exercise) linked to the pandemic and social isolation, where academic pressure 'fuels' this loop, and sees a solution as a 'fresh start' and reset after the courses are done.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from immediate behavioral change by externalizing the cause to the pandemic and framing the solution as a future reset after courses end.
Minimizes the severity of current struggles by emphasizing past success ('marks have been good') and a sense of impending control ('getting a grip on it again').

ambivalence.for_change: Feels guilty about bad habits and not performing as well as they should, and desires to 'break my bad cycles' and get back to normalcy.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Feels an emotional attachment to the late-night, isolated work rhythm as a familiar, if punishing, identity forged during the pandemic, making a shift feel like losing a coping mechanism.

values_and_stakes: Academic performance and the 'good marks' they have historically achieved.
The anticipated 'fresh start' and normalcy of life routines planned for after the courses.
(inferred) The sense of control and dedication built through the 'third round of studying' and the all-nighter grind, which risks being undermined by changing approach mid-stream.
key_facts: The client is on their 'third go through the entire course' to keep knowledge fresh.
They have one week to get through 6 units of readings, finish an assignment, and manage another course's workload due next month.
Their productive window for focused work often arrives around 3 or 4 AM, by which time they are too tired and sleepy to capitalize on it.

background: (inferred) An adult experiencing significant anxiety about the pandemic and economic downturn, likely employed or in a role requiring discipline, and living in a region with seasonal daylight changes.
self_view_of_problem: I am really worried about the future, specifically how the pandemic will play out, and it keeps me up at night.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Deflects by agreeing with generalities ('we are all in the same boat') when therapist probes for specific worries.
(inferred) Shifts focus to external validation ('those around me dont understand my anxiety') when discussing self-control strategies.
(inferred) Uses premature agreement ('I will take your advice') to avoid deeper exploration of personal emotional patterns.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to be informed but not deluged, indicating a desire to manage anxiety without complete disengagement.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I am attached to the identity of being the disciplined, focused one who understands the seriousness better than others.

values_and_stakes: The ability to be informed and prepared about world events.
The perception of being disciplined and focused, especially during a crisis.
(inferred) Trusting relationships with people around me, which feel threatened if they don't understand my anxiety.
key_facts: The client identifies short days as a major depressant.
The client feels those around them don't understand their anxiety.
The client states 'Now is the time to focus and be disciplined' immediately after the therapist describes playful, refreshing breaks.

background: A student finishing their studies during the pandemic, living in an apartment building, working once or twice a week not during the day. (inferred) They have regular phone contact with friends and family.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as a 'vicious circle' of abnormal sleep patterns, lack of motivation, and social isolation, which they see as partly a 'really bad habit' and partly a necessary, stubborn sacrifice for safety during the pandemic.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions for change (like going outdoors) by citing external justifications (pandemic safety, work schedule) and labeling their own stance as 'stubborn thinking'.
Uses comparative victimization ('others in my apartment building are walking freely') and moral reasoning ('sacrificing myself') to justify maintaining isolating behaviors.
(inferred) Minimizes the urgency of change by emphasizing adaptation ('I am kind of used to this endless cycle') and projecting hope into a distant future.

ambivalence.for_change: They admit disappointment in their sleep habits and recognize the damaging cycle, expressing a desire to break the pattern.
ambivalence.against_change: They are emotionally attached to a self-image of stringent, uncompromising sacrifice for the collective good, which justifies their isolation and inertia.

values_and_stakes: Their sense of moral integrity and identity as someone 'doing this for everyone' is at risk if they compromise their stringent safety rules.
The established, low-effort routine of late nights (watching movies, computer use) provides a predictable structure they would lose by changing sleep patterns.
(inferred) Their current social role with friends and family—where pandemic concerns are the primary shared topic—could be disrupted if their daily reality changes.
key_facts: Their sleep pattern is a self-described 'vicious circle' of staying up late and waking up late, which they have not broken.
They go out only for personal errands once every week or two weeks and state they are 'not prepared to go out even for walks'.
Their city is just beginning its second wave of the pandemic as of about two weeks ago.

background: Works in an industry that was previously stable, at a company that had not done layoffs in a long time before COVID. (inferred) Lives independently, responsible for paying bills and keeping a roof over their head.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is the threat of losing their job due to COVID-related layoffs, which is terrifying because they love routine and predictability, and they dread repeating a difficult, six-month job search process.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions for contingency plans (like temp work) with passive hope ('I would hope so'), maintaining a focus on the feared outcome rather than solutions.

Rejects reassurance by immediately refocusing on past negative experiences ('It's just not something I want to go through again'), anchoring their identity as someone who has already endured a traumatic job hunt.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) They feel a pull toward accepting the possibility of change and utilizing support, as evidenced by their expressed appreciation for the therapist's empathy and stating they feel better.
ambivalence.against_change: They are emotionally attached to their routine, predictability, and the hard-won stability of their current job, viewing any disruption as a profound threat to their sense of security.

values_and_stakes: Financial independence and security (paying bills, keeping a roof over their head).
Professional stability and the predictability of their daily routine.
The psychological safety of not having to re-enter a dreaded, lengthy job-hunting process.
key_facts: In a previous job search, it took over 300 applications, 50 interviews, and more than 6 months to find a job.
They have only been at their current job for 18 months.
Their company is talking about more layoffs in a few months.

background: (inferred) A person living alone with a dog, likely employed but experiencing financial constraints, navigating life during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
self_view_of_problem: I've been feeling really sad lately and think I have depression, which existed before 2020 but has been made much worse by the events of this year.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions by citing external barriers (e.g., friends being too busy, lack of money for therapy).
Minimizes engagement with offered solutions by giving brief, non-committal agreement (e.g., 'Right. Online courses are fun', 'Yeah...').

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to feel better and am seeking tips or tricks for things I can do by myself to improve my mood.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is a passive attachment to the current state, where the sadness feels entrenched and external circumstances (2020, finances) justify inaction.

values_and_stakes: The caregiving relationship and routine with her dog, which provides a reason to get out of bed.
(inferred) Financial stability, as spending money on therapy is currently seen as unaffordable.
(inferred) Social connections with friends, which are valued but currently deprioritized due to busy schedules.
key_facts: The client gets out of bed on difficult days specifically for her dog.
The client has identified a lack of money as the reason for not seeking a therapist.
The client frames 2020 as a major exacerbating factor for her pre-existing sadness.

background: (inferred) Likely an adult with a long-term friend from college, has a sister and family support network, engaged in discussions about current events like Covid and the election.
self_view_of_problem: Does not view themselves as having a problem; they see their role as supporting a friend undergoing heart surgery, and feel they have adequate family support without needing professional help.
resistance_drivers: Deflects or minimizes when therapist suggests additional coping or professional help by emphasizing existing support systems.
Shifts focus away from personal emotional needs by redirecting conversation to the friend's situation or external topics like Covid and the election.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) Acknowledges the stress of the situation and the importance of being there for their friend, suggesting a pull toward maintaining connection and support.
ambivalence.against_change: Feels that seeking professional help is unnecessary because family support is sufficient, indicating a pull away from viewing personal coping as inadequate.

values_and_stakes: The 20-year friendship with the friend undergoing surgery, which includes a shared history and mutual support.
Family relationships, particularly with their sister, who provides understanding and support.
(inferred) Their self-identity as a loyal and capable friend who provides emotional support without needing external help.
key_facts: The client has known the friend for 20 years since college, including a brief past romantic relationship.
The client explicitly stated they do not feel the need for professional help because they have enough family support.
The client discusses external stressors like Covid and the election with the friend, indicating a pattern of focusing on broader topics rather than personal emotions.

background: A person grieving the loss of their fiancé who died four years ago from kidney failure; they work from home and have diabetes. (inferred)
self_view_of_problem: Defines the problem as overwhelming sadness and depression, especially on the anniversary, stemming from missing him and feeling the loss of his unconditional love.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions for change by citing physical limitations or recent injuries (e.g., clumsiness, diabetes).
Minimizes the feasibility of new activities by focusing on logistical barriers (e.g., working from home prevents sharing baked goods).

ambivalence.for_change: Wants to feel better and acknowledges that talking helps and that time is healing, even if slowly.
ambivalence.against_change: Fears that moving forward might mean losing the special connection and identity formed by being his 'sunshiney baby doll' who was loved unconditionally.

values_and_stakes: The unique identity and sense of being perfectly loved that came from the relationship with her fiancé.
The ritual of shared, quiet domesticity (curling up on the couch, watching movies) that defined their time together.
(inferred) The safety of familiar grief patterns, which protect her from the risk of new failures or injuries in trying new things.
key_facts: Today is the four-year anniversary of her fiancé's death, which triggers acute grief.
She has diabetes, which limits her dietary choices like baking.
She recently scalded her foot with chili, reinforcing a self-view of clumsiness.

background: (inferred) A person with friends and social connections, likely a student or young adult given the context of texting and concerns about friendship dynamics.
self_view_of_problem: I automatically assume I'm valueless in the other person's eyes, no matter what they say or do to the contrary, and I feel frustrated and sad about my worthiness.
resistance_drivers: Minimizes the problem after verbalizing it (e.g., says it 'sounds not nearly as bad' after typing it out).
Deflects by seeking external advice rather than exploring internal feelings (e.g., asks 'What do you think I should do' instead of reflecting).

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to feel worthy and secure in my friendships, not consumed by feelings of being ignored.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Changing would require challenging a core self-view of being 'valueless,' which feels deeply true and protective.

values_and_stakes: The specific friendship where the friend doesn't reply for hours, risking perceived enthusiasm and connection.
(inferred) A self-image as someone who is not 'self-involved,' which would be threatened by acknowledging the pattern more fully.
key_facts: The client texts a friend who doesn't reply for hours, triggering feelings of being ignored and unworthy.
The client states, 'I always assume since I'm not busy that they aren't too,' revealing a cognitive pattern of projection.
The client has decent phone conversations with the friend, indicating the friendship has positive interactions beyond texting.

background: (inferred) A medical professional applying for a medical fellowship, married to a supportive husband.
self_view_of_problem: I have constant anxiety about my future and job applications, and I feel insecure that I will not get the job I want.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Minimizes or deflects external suggestions for practical support (e.g., job centers, talking to peers/counselors) by highlighting the uniqueness of her situation.
(inferred) Accepts reassurance about working hard but does not elaborate on specific stressors, suggesting a pattern of polite agreement without deeper engagement.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to find a path forward and alleviate the overwhelming stress of the application process.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) My anxiety and stress feel like a necessary, protective part of my identity as a diligent person, contrasting with my husband's more easygoing approach.

values_and_stakes: My self-image as a hardworking and diligent medical professional.
The dynamic in my marriage, where my husband sees me as stressing too much.
(inferred) My desired future career trajectory and securing the specific fellowship I want.
key_facts: The anxiety started about three months ago when she began researching programs and the application process.
She states her husband is supportive but thinks she stresses too much.
She has identified that there are other people in her position or counselors she could talk to.

background: (inferred) A student in a specialized field of study, likely in higher education, who is at risk of academic failure.
self_view_of_problem: I'm close to failing out of school and I don't know what to do; I just can't seem to do well no matter how hard I try.
resistance_drivers: Prefers to externalize the problem by citing a lack of available resources (e.g., 'there arn't any good tutoring services for my field of study') rather than exploring personal action.
Expresses hesitation and seeks reassurance before committing to a suggested action (e.g., asking 'do you think they would help me?' about professors).

ambivalence.for_change: I'm very frustrated at myself and scared about failing, which motivates me to seek solutions.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear that taking direct action (like asking professors) might confirm personal inadequacy or lead to rejection.

values_and_stakes: Academic standing and progression in their specialized field of study.
(inferred) Self-esteem and identity as a competent, capable student.
(inferred) Financial investment in their education, as implied by 'I can't afford to fail my courses'.
key_facts: The client has not yet spoken to their professors about their struggles.
The client has already looked for tutoring services and found them inadequate for their field.
The client is facing imminent exams that will determine if they pass or fail.

background: (inferred) A person with a previously strong social support group, whose life has been disrupted by pandemic lockdowns, likely living alone or apart from close friends.
self_view_of_problem: I'm sad because I haven't been able to see my friends in a long time since the lockdown; my strong social support group has been cut off.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by shifting focus to the therapist's situation when asked about their own sadness.
Agrees with suggestions superficially ('Yeah thats a great idea') but immediately cites a practical barrier ('Its just hard to find time to interact with them').

ambivalence.for_change: I feel sad and miss my friends, and I want to feel connected again.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear that initiating change (organizing contact) will be burdensome, fail to replicate in-person connection, or highlight the ongoing loss.

values_and_stakes: The specific, pre-pandemic in-person friendships and social support group.
The health and safety of friends and their families from COVID-19 infection.
(inferred) Their identity as a considerate friend who doesn't burden others or take unnecessary risks.
key_facts: The client states they have not heard from their friends in a while.
The client says it is hard to find time to interact with friends.
The client ends the session planning to try organizing an online get-together.

background: First-year college student living on campus with a roommate, attending virtual classes during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown.
self_view_of_problem: I'm lonely because I lost all my friends when school went virtual, and my roommate is busy with her boyfriend, leaving me on my own all the time.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions for on-campus socializing by citing external constraints (e.g., lockdown, clubs not active).
Minimizes the severity of her emotional state to others, especially parents, to avoid causing worry.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to feel less lonely and reconnect with people, which is why I'm open to planning a virtual party and calling my parents.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I am attached to the idea that my loneliness is an unavoidable, pandemic-wide condition, which reduces my sense of personal agency to change it.

values_and_stakes: My parents' approval and emotional stability — I risk upsetting them and damaging our relationship if I drop out or fully express my distress.
My social connections with high school friends — I risk losing these relationships if I don't maintain them during physical separation.
(inferred) My identity as a capable, independent college student — I risk seeing myself as a failure if I quit school.
key_facts: The client's roommate has a boyfriend and goes on hikes with him, leaving the client alone.
The client has already tried solitary activities like painting and finds schoolwork very easy.
The client's mother is a social person working from home, which the client believes is probably hard for her too.

background: (inferred) A person who has recently moved to a new city and is experiencing financial strain due to unpaid loans from friends.
self_view_of_problem: I am owed a lot of money by my friends but they aren't paying me back, blaming covid, and I see them spending on personal goods instead of returning the money, which puts me in a tight spot financially.
resistance_drivers: Deflects direct questions about the friends' borrowing history by focusing on their current non-payment.
Expresses reluctance to escalate to family or confront friends aggressively due to fear of losing the friendship.

ambivalence.for_change: I don't like them taking undue advantage of me either, and I need the cash to pay my bills.
ambivalence.against_change: I don't want to lose my friends, because they are the only people that helped me when I shifted to this city.

values_and_stakes: The financial security and ability to pay bills that depends on recovering the loaned cash.
The friendship and social support network from these friends in a new city.
(inferred) Self-respect and the principle of not being taken advantage of in relationships.
key_facts: The client loaned hard cash and needs repayment in cash, not digital transfers.
The client has seen the friends spending money on personal goods instead of repaying.
Due to lockdown restrictions, the client is unable to travel places easily.

background: (inferred) A person who has been involved in a legal case regarding abuse, with former friends who sided with the abuser.
self_view_of_problem: I'm having a hard time dealing with hurtful things people have said to me, and I feel no self-worth.
resistance_drivers: Deflects or changes the subject when asked about direct communication or action (e.g., when therapist asks about telling people how their words hurt).
(inferred) Withdraws or becomes apologetic when there is a miscommunication or perceived demand (e.g., apologizing for not receiving a message).

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to feel less alone and stressed, and to have my self-worth restored.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Engaging directly with the hurtful people or the situation feels impossible and risks further isolation or legal violation.

values_and_stakes: A sense of justice and validation from the legal case, which is threatened if former friends side with the abuser.
Social connections and support, which are at risk due to isolation from former friends.
(inferred) Personal safety and legal compliance, which would be jeopardized by contacting people involved in the case.
key_facts: Former friends have remained friends with the person who abused the client and stood up for them in court.
A legal order prohibits anyone involved in the case from speaking to each other.
The client explicitly states, 'I feel no self-worth.'

background: She is a mother with school-aged boys, married to a controlling husband who tracks her activities and prevents her from seeking treatment for her depression. (inferred) She was diagnosed with Major Clinical Depression over 20 years ago.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as 'anger issues and thinking nasty thoughts toward my husband' caused by 'how he treats me lately,' specifically his disrespectful and sexually demeaning comments.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions by immediately citing her husband's control as an absolute barrier (e.g., 'there is no way I can' when told to seek treatment secretly).
Uses past failed attempts and feared consequences (like losing her children) as proof that action is futile, shutting down discussion of change.

ambivalence.for_change: She admits 'its time for a change' and feels better when supported, showing a desire to stop being treated disrespectfully.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She is pulled away from change by a paralyzing fear of her husband's retaliation, including using her depression and house photos to prove she is an unfit mom and take her boys.

values_and_stakes: Custody of and relationship with her sons, which he has threatened to take.
Her identity and standing as a competent mother and homemaker, which he attacks with photos and insults.
(inferred) The stability and structure of her family unit, which leaving or confronting him would dismantle.
key_facts: Her husband has photos of a dirty house and her depression diagnosis, which he would use in a custody battle.
He tracks everything she does, preventing her from seeking therapy secretly.
She has threatened to leave him years ago, and he responded by threatening to take the boys.

background: (inferred) A student who has been isolated from friends since March due to the pandemic and academic workload.
self_view_of_problem: I'm sad that I haven't been able to see any of my friends since March, and I just wish we could hang out again.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Initially dismisses suggested solutions (like Zoom for socializing) by citing external constraints (studies, lack of time).
(inferred) Shows passive agreement without immediate commitment, requiring repeated therapist encouragement before considering change.

ambivalence.for_change: I think chatting with my friends and seeing them online will hopefully make me feel better.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A reluctance to adopt new, unfamiliar technologies for personal connection, preferring the familiar, in-person interactions that feel lost.

values_and_stakes: The quality and closeness of friendships maintained through direct, in-person contact.
(inferred) The sense of normalcy and social belonging that comes from routine, physical hangouts with friends.
key_facts: The client has not seen friends in person since March.
The client uses Zoom for class but has never used it to chat with friends.
The client messages friends on Facebook once in a while but they haven't chatted much.

background: A 66-year-old person whose immediate family is deceased, has no children, and is in touch only with a troubled cousin; has limited friends and is on antidepressant medication.
self_view_of_problem: Feels a sense of uselessness and fear of death, exacerbated by current sad conditions including COVID isolation and the burden of a troubled cousin.
resistance_drivers: Redirects focus from personal distress to the cousin's dire situation when therapist suggests self-care.
Accepts suggestions politely but quickly moves to close the session, avoiding deeper exploration of personal emotional pain.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) Wants relief from sadness and isolation, as indicated by reaching out for therapy and acknowledging the therapist's suggestions as good.
ambivalence.against_change: Feels a moral obligation not to abandon the cousin, viewing self-care as potentially equivalent to the abandonment others have committed.

values_and_stakes: The role as the sole remaining supportive family member for her troubled cousin.
(inferred) A sense of identity tied to enduring hardship and not being someone who abandons family.
(inferred) The stability of her current coping routine, including medication management, which COVID has disrupted.
key_facts: The client's cousin is in a homeless women's shelter with a bipolar diagnosis and likely borderline personality disorder.
The client is on antidepressant medication but finds it hard to keep in touch with the provider due to COVID.
The client ended the session on a positive note after receiving a resource link, preferring to close rather than delve deeper.

background: (inferred) A professional who recently started a new job, likely in a competitive or demanding field, and is navigating a new work environment.
self_view_of_problem: I feel like I'm constantly trying to prove myself, measure myself against other people, and just don't feel I'm good enough; I'm having a real issue with my confidence at the moment.
resistance_drivers: Deflects reassurance by shifting to another perceived inadequacy (e.g., from results to organization).
Seeks external validation by asking if the therapist can relate, rather than exploring their own feelings directly.

ambivalence.for_change: I've worked really hard to get a better position and want to be successful, not feel like a failure.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear that acknowledging the job is too much confirms a personal inadequacy and means giving up on a hard-won achievement.

values_and_stakes: The specific new job and position they worked hard to attain.
Self-image as a competent, successful professional who can measure up.
(inferred) Potential future career progression and opportunities tied to succeeding in this role.
key_facts: The client compares their results to those of co-workers they perceive as more experienced and smarter.
The client states they will give the job 'a good few weeks' and then reassess how they think they are doing.
The client feels their work is so complicated they sometimes wonder if they've bitten off more than they can chew.

background: (inferred) A person in a long-term romantic relationship, recently separated from their partner due to pandemic lockdowns.
self_view_of_problem: My longtime partner cheated on me recently and I just found out; it's been such a hard couple of months because of the virus, and now with this I just don't know what to do.
resistance_drivers: Minimizes own needs and avoids seeking support, stating 'I don't want to bother anyone' when therapist suggests reaching out to friends or family.
Defers to therapist for direction and solutions, repeatedly asking 'what else do you think I should do?' rather than generating their own steps.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) A desire to feel better and resolve the sadness, as indicated by agreeing to try the therapist's suggestions and stating 'I feel a little better now'.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) An emotional pull toward isolation and self-protection, avoiding vulnerability by not sharing the pain with close others.

values_and_stakes: The long-term relationship with their partner, which is now ended due to the betrayal.
(inferred) Trust in future romantic relationships, as the client states they won't be able to trust this partner again.
(inferred) Social connections with friends or family, which are at risk of neglect due to the client's reluctance to 'bother' them.
key_facts: The client's partner cheated during the pandemic lockdown, a period when they hadn't been able to see each other.
The client has not spoken to anyone else about the infidelity before this session.
The client explicitly states they will not return to the partner because 'They've hurt me too much and I won't be able to trust them again'.

background: (inferred) A person living in the North of the UK near Manchester, subject to coronavirus lockdown restrictions and social isolation.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as being 'put in such a sad emotional state' by the lockdowns and restrictions, with low motivation, and wonders why they are dealing with it worse than their friends.
resistance_drivers: Questions the therapist's personal experience with depression to gauge applicability before accepting advice.
Expresses uncertainty about whether the problem is situational ('goes a little bit deeper than this'), potentially deflecting simple solutions.

ambivalence.for_change: They acknowledge that virtual socializing 'would definitely work to boost my mood' and are interested in trying new activities like a virtual book club.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear that acknowledging a deeper, unfamiliar depressive state could be overwhelming or define their identity.

values_and_stakes: The sense of normalcy and emotional resilience compared to friends who 'seem to be dealing with it better'.
(inferred) The stability of their pre-pandemic self-image as someone not familiar with depression.
The practical ability to maintain social connections with friends they haven't seen.
key_facts: The client is currently not mixing with people outside their household due to restrictions.
The client has never heard of the Meetup app before.
The client finds the therapist's suggestion of a Zoom party to be 'a really good suggestion'.

background: (inferred) The client is employed in a workplace with a manager and other managers, and they rely on their job for steady income.
