self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as receiving 'ridiculous' and 'petty' feedback from a manager who 'just doesn't like me' and 'has it out for me,' which is frustrating and not constructive work-based feedback.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by externalizing blame onto the manager's character ('she just doesn't like me') when the therapist suggests direct communication or resolution.
Shifts to considering structural solutions (going to another manager, transferring) when faced with the emotional risk of confronting the manager directly.
Minimizes the problem's significance ('perhaps I'm just making too much of a big deal') when the therapist validates their feelings, suggesting a pattern of backing down from conflict.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) The client desires to resolve the hurt and frustration caused by the feedback to improve their work environment.
ambivalence.against_change: The client fears that addressing the feedback directly could damage their working relationship with the manager and jeopardize their needed steady income.

values_and_stakes: A stable working relationship with their current manager.
Their current job position and the steady income it provides.
(inferred) Their self-image as a positive, non-confrontational person in the workplace.
key_facts: The client's manager gave feedback criticizing how the client sits and smiles in meetings.
The client is actively considering complaining to a different manager or transferring positions.
The client acknowledges they have taken the feedback very personally.

background: (inferred) The client is a student who lives with family and has been attending school online since March due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as not doing as well in school since COVID, feeling down and unmotivated, and being upset and ashamed at themselves for it.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Minimizes personal responsibility by externalizing the problem to the pandemic ('the virus has been hard on everyone hasn't it').
(inferred) Expresses agreement with suggestions but emphasizes practical barriers ('I find I don't have a lot of time for them', 'Its hard to fine time but I should try').

ambivalence.for_change: The client acknowledges that changing their environment and routines might help alleviate their down feelings and lack of motivation.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The client is attached to the hope that external circumstances (vaccine development, a return to normal) will solve their problems, reducing the internal urgency to change.

values_and_stakes: Academic performance and success in school.
Maintaining connections with friends ('I really miss seeing all my buddies at school').
(inferred) Preserving a sense of self-worth and avoiding shame associated with their current struggles.
key_facts: The client has not seen anyone in person other than family since March.
The client works in the basement and doesn't get much sunlight.
The client has picked up a couple of hobbies but finds little time for them due to school.

background: The client worked in live audio and carpentry in the music industry before being laid off due to Covid-19, is immunocompromised, and is currently unemployed, financially stressed, and living off loans from friends and art sales while seeking work.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as being 'terribly stuck' in limbo, unable to safely work or qualify for other jobs while waiting for their old industry to reopen and their old job to return.
resistance_drivers: Deflects or changes the subject when the therapist suggests emotional processing (e.g., mourning the past) by pivoting to practical survival or task completion.
Uses future-oriented hope (e.g., a vaccine and job return) to avoid engaging with present emotional distress or alternative plans.
(inferred) Minimizes or downplays their own distress by focusing on polite, task-oriented exchanges and affirming the therapist rather than deepening self-exploration.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) They feel scattered and stressed by the current limbo, wanting their life back and to feel accomplished, which pulls them toward seeking stability and relief.
ambivalence.against_change: They are emotionally attached to their pre-pandemic identity and career path, fearing that letting go of that hope would mean losing their planned future and sense of self.

values_and_stakes: Their pre-pandemic career in live audio and carpentry, which represents their professional identity and a 'really good career path'.
Financial survival and independence, currently at risk as they rely on loans from friends and uncertain art sales.
Their physical health and safety, as being immunocompromised limits their work options and makes returning to in-person work risky.
key_facts: The client has been assured they will get their old job back if their company reopens in early 2021.
The client has not received any government financial assistance and is living off loans from friends.
The client is immunocompromised, restricting them to computer-based work for safety.

background: A woman who was in a nearly 5-year relationship and lived with her boyfriend, who controlled all shared finances; she is now broke, without a place to stay, and temporarily staying with a friend.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as a practical crisis: her boyfriend broke up with her, leaving her with no money and no place to stay, which makes her feel really depressed and overwhelmed.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Information not available in transcript.

ambivalence.for_change: She feels better talking about her situation and laying it all out, as it makes it easier to figure her stuff out and she understands what she needs to do.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The emotional pull away from change may be a fear of fully confronting the grief and identity loss from the end of a 5-year relationship, preferring to focus on immediate logistics.

values_and_stakes: Her immediate safety and shelter are at risk, as she can only stay with her friend for 2 more days.
Her financial independence and stability are at risk, as she currently has no money of her own.
Her connection to family support is at risk, as she needs to get 150 miles to her mom's house to have a stable place.
key_facts: She is waiting to hear back from Capital One about getting approved for a credit card.
Her friend can loan her $70, but the bus ticket to her mom costs $150.
She was in a relationship for almost 5 years where all money was in her boyfriend's name.

background: The client is a pharmacy student studying to become a pharmacist, who will soon be working in hospitals and is concerned about friends in the same field.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as anxiety about their job future due to COVID-19, specifically citing colleagues having trouble getting licenses and the risk of getting sick from working in hospitals.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Deflects or minimizes personal anxiety when the therapist offers optimistic reassurances, shifting focus to general concerns.
(inferred) Avoids deeper exploration of personal fears by agreeing with therapist's broad statements without elaborating on own emotional experience.

ambivalence.for_change: The client wants to reduce anxiety and secure their professional future, hoping vaccines will allow a return to normal.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is an emotional pull to maintain worry as a form of preparedness and identity as a responsible future healthcare worker facing real dangers.

values_and_stakes: Their career path and ability to work as a pharmacist, which depends on obtaining a license and avoiding illness.
The safety and well-being of their friends who will also be working in hospitals.
(inferred) Their sense of purpose and ability to help others, which is tied to working in healthcare.
key_facts: The client is studying to be a pharmacist and will soon work in hospitals.
Colleagues are having trouble getting licenses due to COVID-19.
The client expresses worry about getting sick and about friends working in hospitals.

background: A person who lost their job due to Covid-19 industry shutdowns, is unemployed, applying for jobs and using services like mturk from home while waiting on unemployment claims, and engages in art as a hobby.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is being financially behind on bills and feeling helpless to change the situation, which has negatively impacted their mood, and being set back from their intended career path.
resistance_drivers: Corrects or clarifies the therapist's suggestions when they oversimplify the problem (e.g., budgeting, time management) by stating the core issue is insufficient income, not lack of effort.
Expresses frustration when long-term self-improvement advice is given, by contrasting it with the immediate, concrete setback to their career and desire to have their life back.

ambivalence.for_change: They feel better when they accomplish something each day, like applying for jobs or doing mturk tasks, and see value in looking ahead and doing more art.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is an emotional pull to surrender to helplessness and just wait for the situation to be over, as acting feels futile against such a large external setback.

values_and_stakes: Their intended career path and professional identity, which the pandemic has derailed.
Financial stability and the ability to cover basic expenses without constant strain.
The ability to genuinely relax and enjoy free time without the pressure of being financially behind.
key_facts: The client spends a good portion of each day applying for jobs and doing mturk tasks to feel accomplished.
The client has been doing a lot more art during this time and wishes someone would buy it for a confidence boost.
The client feels they have done everything they can for the day and then struggles with feeling stir-crazy.

background: (inferred) A man living away from his family in another country, currently employed.
self_view_of_problem: I am depressed because my girlfriend is cheating on me with my friend, which makes me feel foolish, betrayed, and helpless.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by externalizing blame onto others (e.g., 'Why are girls like this?') when confronted with his own helplessness.
Shifts focus to revenge fantasies when therapist suggests moving on or positive distraction.
(inferred) Minimizes his own destructive actions (breaking phone, damaging credit card) by not reflecting on them as part of the problem.

ambivalence.for_change: He acknowledges that moving on is the right path and feels a pull toward a better life with his new job.
ambivalence.against_change: He is emotionally attached to the anger and desire for revenge, which gives him a sense of agency and masks his helplessness.

values_and_stakes: His sense of justice and personal dignity, which feels violated and demands rectification.
His social standing and pride in front of his girlfriend and friend, which he feels must be restored through visible success.
(inferred) His self-image as a trusting and loyal partner, which is now shattered and risks being replaced by a view of himself as a fool.
key_facts: He broke his phone in anger and damaged her credit card.
His family is in another country and he cannot visit due to COVID.
He just got a much better job while his friend was fired.

background: (inferred) A person living with family during the COVID-19 pandemic, likely with increased time at home due to social distancing measures.
self_view_of_problem: I have been feeling a bit down lately, with higher levels of stress and concern since the pandemic began, and I struggle with feeling more down than I'd like.
resistance_drivers: Prefers self-management and rejects the need for formal intervention, as shown by stating 'I don't feel I'm at a level that I need therapy or medication'.
(inferred) Seeks low-risk, home-based solutions, as shown by asking for activities 'without risking my health' and 'in my own home'.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to find ways to calm my nerves when I am feeling apprehensive or stressed out and get out of a rut with the same activities.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is a comfort and safety in familiar, home-based routines that avoids the perceived risk or effort of more significant change.

values_and_stakes: The safety and health of myself and my loved ones from COVID-19.
Positive connection and time spent with my family at home.
(inferred) A sense of personal control and competence in managing my own emotional state without external help.
key_facts: The client has tried getting their mind off stress by spending time with family and previously tried meditation.
The client finds social media can make them feel better through humor but can also be depressing.
The client used to read quite a bit more but has slowed down on it.

background: (inferred) The client works in a small office with a part-time coworker and a boss they have previously spoken to about workplace issues.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as 'anxiety related to my job' caused by a specific coworker who is 'very unhelpful and hypocritical,' 'tries to boss me around,' and is rude and interruptive.
resistance_drivers: Deflects direct action by externalizing the problem onto the coworker's personality ('aggressive personality') and predicting her departure ('she may not be working here that much longer').
Minimizes the problem's severity and his own agency by focusing on coping strategies ('relax and relieve stress in other outlets') rather than addressing the interpersonal conflict.
(inferred) Avoids escalating the issue through formal channels (like HR) by citing the small office structure and prior inaction from his boss.

ambivalence.for_change: He acknowledges a need to 'find a better way to deal with the situation' and values having 'another opinion on the subject.'
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is emotionally attached to avoiding confrontation and the discomfort of taking direct action, preferring to wait out the problem or manage his internal reaction.

values_and_stakes: Maintaining a low-stress, conflict-free daily work environment in his small office.
Preserving his current coping routines and personal comfort, like snacking and avoiding the gym.
(inferred) Protecting his self-image as someone who handles stress without letting it 'get to me or take it personally.'
key_facts: The client has already mentioned the issue to his boss before with no apparent resolution.
The problematic coworker is now only part-time.
The client uses humor and deflection when discussing his own avoidance ('I am trying to force myself to go to the gym... haha').

background: A college student majoring in Psychology with a minor in Biology, who is a parent to a 2-year-old son and is nearing graduation in June.
self_view_of_problem: I failed my finals and am on academic probation, which is scary because I'm near graduation and I hate online courses; the pandemic is wearing me out.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Minimizes personal agency by attributing struggles to external factors like the pandemic and online courses.
(inferred) Expresses self-criticism (feeling like a failure) when considering adaptive changes like dropping a minor.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to finally finish my Bachelor's and do something positive.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear that changing my academic plan (like dropping a minor) confirms a personal failure rather than being a strategic adjustment.

values_and_stakes: Graduating with a Bachelor's degree in June.
Maintaining the identity of a capable student and parent who can handle difficult courses.
(inferred) The well-being and stability provided for her 2-year-old son.
key_facts: She failed her finals and is on academic probation, with the decision likely in the next week.
She has already registered for classes next semester but is considering dropping her Biology minor.
She learned about failing her finals yesterday, and the semester is shorter due to the pandemic.

background: (inferred) A parent going through a divorce, living far from family, with two children and needing to stay in their current location to keep the children close to their father.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as a difficult divorce involving conflict over child support and visitation, compounded by living far from family support.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Shifts focus from emotional distress to practical constraints when probed about deeper feelings or support needs.
(inferred) Avoids exploring the emotional impact of isolation by emphasizing logistical or external barriers.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) The client desires emotional support and connection, as indicated by valuing contact even over Zoom/phone.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The pull away from change is the fear of disrupting the children's stability and proximity to their father.

values_and_stakes: The stability and proximity of her children to their father.
Maintaining family connections despite physical distance.
(inferred) Preserving a sense of parental responsibility and control during the divorce process.
key_facts: The client is going through a divorce with conflict over child support and visitation.
The client lives far from all family and has no local support.
The client has two children and feels she must stay in her location to keep them close to their father.

background: (inferred) A parent who has been a long-term caregiver for children and is currently unemployed, struggling financially.
self_view_of_problem: I can't find a job because I've been staying home with the children for so many years and lack experience, which makes me feel ashamed and stressed about paying bills.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Expresses uncertainty and seeks external validation when presented with potential solutions (e.g., asking 'Where do I find them?' and 'Do you have experience with one?').
(inferred) Shows hesitation by questioning the efficacy of suggested methods (e.g., doubting if a recruiter works as well as a regular application).

ambivalence.for_change: I want to find a job or start a business to alleviate financial stress and shame.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear that changing my role from caregiver to job-seeker or entrepreneur will expose my lack of experience and lead to failure or rejection.

values_and_stakes: The ability to pay bills and avoid financial shame.
The role as a caregiver for my children, which I want to maintain while pursuing work.
(inferred) My self-worth and identity tied to being a capable provider and parent.
key_facts: The client has been a caregiver for children for many years, creating a gap in work experience.
The client expresses shame about not being able to pay bills.
The client shows interest in starting a business from home to still care for the kids.

background: (inferred) A person living in a small apartment, likely working or studying, who experiences depressive episodes at night and is affected by daylight savings time.
self_view_of_problem: I get severely depressed at nighttime and have almost mental breakdowns about everything in my life, but it doesn't happen all the time and I don't know why.
resistance_drivers: Expresses fear of opening up to a stranger, which may block seeking professional help.
(inferred) Minimizes the problem's severity by emphasizing it only happens 'sometimes' and 'only at night', potentially avoiding deeper exploration.
(inferred) Deflects from structured advice by focusing on practical barriers (e.g., small apartment, accustomed sleep schedule) rather than emotional roots.

ambivalence.for_change: I really want to try new things to help and feel motivated after receiving advice.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear that seeking help or changing routines will expose vulnerability and make me appear weak to others.

values_and_stakes: My sense of strength and not appearing weak to others.
My current sleep schedule and daily routine, which I am accustomed to.
(inferred) The comfort and safety of my small apartment environment, where I retreat during episodes.

The client has not yet tried therapy due to fear of opening up to a stranger.
The client lives in a small apartment and has noticed that moving from bed to the couch changes their environment.

background: A mother with two sons, married, living within 20 minutes of her own mother who does not drive. (inferred) She was accustomed to seeing her mother at least once a week before the pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is not being able to see, hug, and spend time with her mother in person due to COVID-19 restrictions enforced by her husband to protect their high-risk family.
resistance_drivers: Deflects or dismisses therapist's attempts to reframe or find alternatives (e.g., rejecting the window-visit idea by emphasizing her husband's distrust).
Uses absolutist language ('forbidden', 'won't let me') when describing her husband's restrictions, framing the situation as immovable.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) She desires the emotional comfort and connection of physical presence with her mother.
ambivalence.against_change: She feels a pull to accept her husband's protective stance because she frames it as him 'protecting us' from a health risk.

values_and_stakes: The physical safety and health of her immediate family (husband and two sons).
Her close, physically affectionate relationship with her mother.
Her role and autonomy as a daughter capable of visiting and caring for her mother.
key_facts: She calls her mother daily but has not seen her in person for over six months.
Her husband does not trust her to follow safety rules if she visits, forbidding in-person contact.
Her oldest son is sad about not seeing his grandmother, while her youngest is preoccupied with Roblox.

background: A man who was in a long-term relationship of over five years and was planning to marry his girlfriend before she cheated on him, leading to a breakup. (inferred) He has a supportive family, including his mother and younger brother.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as a heartbreak from being cheated on by the girlfriend he was supposed to marry, leaving him sad, unsure what to do, and doubting if he can ever trust a woman again.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Shifts focus to immediate coping actions (like going to his mother's or making a drink) when the therapist suggests self-care or future optimism, avoiding deeper emotional processing.
(inferred) Minimizes his emotional pain by emphasizing family support as a solution, potentially deflecting from fully acknowledging his grief and trust issues.

ambivalence.for_change: He seeks assistance and advice, indicating a desire to feel better and find a way forward after the breakup.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is emotionally attached to the identity of being betrayed and heartbroken, which protects him from the vulnerability of trusting someone new.

values_and_stakes: The trust and safety he once felt in a long-term romantic relationship, which he now sees as broken.
His reliance on family (mother and brother) as his primary emotional support system, which he might risk if he moves toward independence or new relationships.
(inferred) His self-image as a committed partner planning marriage, which he would have to redefine if he fully accepts the relationship is over.
key_facts: He was in the relationship for over five years and was planning to marry his girlfriend.
He is driving three hours to his mother's house to talk things over.
He mentions making himself a drink to calm his nerves during the conversation.

background: (inferred) A person who is the primary support for a close friend struggling with alcoholism, likely not a professional caregiver but a friend or family member deeply invested in the relationship.
self_view_of_problem: I have a friend who is an alcoholic and just can't seem to quit drinking, and I do not know how to help them anymore.
resistance_drivers: Rejects suggestions that involve distancing from the friend by immediately asserting the friend's need for their support.
Expresses worry about the friend's reaction to seeking external support (like Al-Anon) if others he knows might find out.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want relief from the exhaustion and helplessness of watching my friend struggle and hurt me.
ambivalence.against_change: I fear that taking necessary steps for my own well-being (like time apart) would only hurt him, because he needs my support.

values_and_stakes: The friendship with this 'wonderful,' 'sweet' person who has a lot to give when sober.
My role as the person closest to him and his primary source of support.
(inferred) My self-image as a kind-hearted, caring person who does not abandon others in need.
key_facts: The friend cycles between quitting for a couple of weeks and then going back to drinking.
The friend becomes argumentative when drinking, which hurts the client.
The client had not previously considered online support options like Al-Anon, thinking attendance at in-person meetings was required.

background: (inferred) A college student who is currently taking online classes and struggling academically.
self_view_of_problem: I'm not doing as well in college as I want to, and I feel underprepared and like I don't really belong here. I have a huge problem with procrastination and a terrible time concentrating.
resistance_drivers: Deflects responsibility by attributing struggles to external circumstances, like online classes making it harder to concentrate and ask questions.
Expresses a need for external guidance and explanation, resisting the internal shift to self-reliance.

ambivalence.for_change: I guess I really do need to make changes because my old high school methods aren't working.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear of losing the familiar identity and competence of being a 'great student' from high school, which is tied to a simpler, more guided way of learning.

values_and_stakes: The valued identity and self-esteem of being a 'great student' that was established in high school.
The concrete academic standing and future prospects tied to succeeding in college.
(inferred) The comfort and security of dependent learning relationships with authority figures like professors.
key_facts: The client was a great student in high school but is now struggling in college.
All of the client's classes are currently online.
The client's procrastination used to work in high school but does not work now.

background: (inferred) An individual involved in a legal dispute with a former friend, currently managing social relationships amid interpersonal conflict.
self_view_of_problem: An ex-friend is talking behind my back to my current friends, and I have a strong constitution about myself and don't allow to be disrespected by anyone.
resistance_drivers: Rejects any suggestion of engagement or mediation with the ex-friend, framing it as unnecessary and past talking.
Deflects from exploring emotional impact or alternative solutions by immediately escalating to legal threats (suing for slander).

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to protect my current friendships and my self-respect from being undermined.
ambivalence.against_change: Changing my approach (like mediating) would feel like allowing disrespect and weakening my strong constitutional stance.

values_and_stakes: Maintaining current friendships, which are at risk if friends take the ex-friend's side.
Upholding a self-image as someone who is strong and does not tolerate disrespect from anyone.
(inferred) Avoiding the emotional vulnerability and potential isolation that might come from confronting the situation more directly.
key_facts: The client and the ex-friend have sued each other in court before, and a previous restraining order was initially granted then weakened.
The client states they will sue the ex-friend for slander if the behavior gets bad enough.
The client will cut off current friends if they take the ex-friend's side.

background: (inferred) A student preparing for an academic presentation, likely in higher education given the context of a career-impacting presentation.
self_view_of_problem: I am stressed about giving a presentation tomorrow, specifically worried about public speaking and my ability to field questions effectively.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Catastrophizes about uncontrollable variables, like all the different types of potential questions, which amplifies stress and blocks acceptance of uncertainty.
(inferred) Seeks excessive control over the situation, indicated by stress over preparing for every eventual question, resisting the therapist's advice to accept limits.

ambivalence.for_change: I desire to perform well and fulfill the assignment, so I am seeking advice to reduce my stress.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear that accepting uncertainty about questions will lead to failure or exposure as not being an expert.

values_and_stakes: My academic career and the success of this important presentation.
(inferred) My self-image as a competent and prepared student who can handle expert scrutiny.
key_facts: The presentation is tomorrow, creating immediate time pressure.
The client identifies fielding questions as a specific stressful factor beyond general public speaking.
The client acknowledges the therapist's advice is good but still reports stress when trying to prepare.

background: (inferred) A person in their late 20s to 30s who has recently experienced a breakup due to a partner's infidelity with a close friend.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is that my partner cheated on me with my close friend, and I mistakenly believed all people have the same good intentions and loyalty.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from personal pain to broad societal critiques when discussing disloyalty (e.g., 'The world is becoming more shallow and unjust by the day').
Seeks external validation and comparative stories (e.g., asking the therapist about their past breakups) rather than exploring own feelings directly.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to move on to a better and more prosperous life and avoid being hurt this badly again.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Holding onto the hurt and anger provides a sense of moral righteousness and protects against the vulnerability of trusting again.

values_and_stakes: The identity of being a loyal friend and partner, which feels betrayed.
The belief in a just and reciprocal social world where people look out for each other.
(inferred) Future close friendships and romantic relationships, which now feel risky and uncertain.
key_facts: The client's partner cheated on them with their close friend.
The client states they have always been a loyal friend and would not jeopardize those relationships.
The client initially expressed a desire for revenge to make their ex-partner regret leaving.

background: (inferred) A married mother with at least two sons, one in kindergarten, managing cyberschooling and household responsibilities while her husband works remotely.
self_view_of_problem: My husband keeps putting me down and calling me names, degrading me and not respecting me, especially in front of our kids, which makes me feel inferior and angry.
resistance_drivers: Deflects responsibility for action onto external constraints, like COVID-19 and family logistics, when therapist suggests practical steps.
Uses sarcasm or dismissive agreement ('Great idea . I think I will') to prematurely end therapeutic engagement when feeling pressured.
(inferred) Minimizes the frequency of the abuse ('He doesnt do it all the time') to rationalize inaction.

ambivalence.for_change: I am so very angry and disgusted with my life and want the disrespect to stop.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fears that confronting the situation directly will escalate the abuse and further damage her standing with her children.

values_and_stakes: Her role and identity as a 'good mom' to her boys, which her husband attacks by calling her a 'worthless mom'.
The stability and daily functioning of her household, which she manages (cyberschooling, homework) and risks disrupting.
(inferred) The marital relationship itself, despite its toxicity, as a primary adult connection in a context of limited social support.
key_facts: Her husband insults her as 'white trash' and a 'worthless mom' in front of their children.
She usually keeps quiet in response to his verbal abuse to avoid escalation.
She had a few hours of 'me time' daily before COVID, which the pandemic eliminated.

background: (inferred) A person who was engaged for two years and in a relationship for almost three years, currently experiencing a recent breakup.
self_view_of_problem: I am sad and devastated about my break up; life is falling apart, and nothing feels good or positive, even when trying to focus on other things or take me time.
resistance_drivers: Rejects positive reframing when therapist offers future-focused optimism, insisting nothing feels good.
Shifts focus to ending the conversation when emotional depth is approached, indicating avoidance of prolonged engagement.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I wish I could turn my love off to be in a better place, indicating a desire to stop hurting.
ambivalence.against_change: Holding onto the emotional pain and love for the ex-partner feels necessary, as letting go threatens the meaning of the past relationship and current identity.

values_and_stakes: The three-year relationship and two-year engagement, representing a significant investment of time and emotional commitment.
The hope for closure or understanding about why the breakup happened, which remains unresolved.
(inferred) The sense of a stable future and life plan that has now been disrupted.
key_facts: The breakup occurred last week, so the emotional impact is very recent and acute.
The client has tried taking 'me time' and focusing on other things, but reports nothing helps.
The client explicitly wishes they could 'turn my love for him off' to feel better.

background: (inferred) The client is a working professional who met Doug at work, and they have been involved in a secret affair for seven months.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as being 'in love with someone' they can't have, stating 'It's not Doug's problem it's mine!' and asking how to 'get rid of the feelings I have for Doug'.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by questioning the therapist's personal experience and qualifications when feeling challenged or not getting direct advice.
Rejects therapist reframing (e.g., focusing on Doug's wife or dishonesty) by insisting the problem is solely their own feelings or Doug's marital status.
(inferred) Minimizes the affair's seriousness by labeling it a 'fling' or 'hook up' while simultaneously acknowledging its long duration and emotional impact.

ambivalence.for_change: The client explicitly states 'I'm ready to end this situation because I want the more emotional stuff I know Doug can't give.'
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The client is emotionally attached to the physical and romantic excitement Doug provides, fearing the loneliness and emptiness of ending it.

values_and_stakes: The secret romantic and sexual relationship with Doug, which makes them 'sing' and feel alive.
(inferred) Their professional reputation and social standing at work, where some colleagues may suspect the relationship.
Their sense of self as a strong, capable person who shouldn't 'settle', which is threatened by accepting the affair's limitations.
key_facts: The affair has lasted seven months, evolving from an intended fling into a sustained emotional attachment.
They work with Doug and have been seen having lunch and taking walks together, increasing the entanglement and risk of exposure.
The client has kept the affair a secret from their friends, isolating their support network.

background: (inferred) The client is an adult with a history of anxiety, who has sought support through groups, therapy, and medication.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as ongoing anxiety that feels overwhelming despite trying support groups, therapy, and medication, and is currently triggered by the scary situation of a friend with possible COVID.
resistance_drivers: Expresses that practical coping strategies feel insufficient when worry is high, stating 'It is hard though because I still worry. Sometimes I feel too worried to do the things necessary to stop it all spiraling'.

(inferred) May subtly externalize the source of anxiety onto the uncontrollable situation (friend's health) rather than internal patterns, as relief is tied to an external outcome: 'the only thing that would ultimately really make me feel better is knowing my friend is okay.'

ambivalence.for_change: The client acknowledges that keeping busy and practicing self-care can help, and is open to techniques like breathing and meditation.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is an emotional pull to maintain worry as a form of connection or vigilance for a vulnerable friend, making it hard to fully engage in self-care that might feel like distraction or abandonment of concern.

values_and_stakes: The health and safety of a friend who already has health issues.
(inferred) Their self-identity as a caring, vigilant person who worries about loved ones.
(inferred) The stability and effectiveness of their existing coping system (support groups, therapy, medication), which risks being seen as inadequate if anxiety persists.
key_facts: The client's friend is going to the hospital today for tests due to possible COVID.
The client describes themselves as 'a worrier anyways'.
The client has previously tried support groups, therapy, and medication for anxiety.

background: A veteran with three children, unmarried, currently working a job without benefits and pursuing a master's degree while on the honor roll.
self_view_of_problem: I have no motivation to work anymore; I lost interest and feel obligated to stay because my boss is a veteran like me.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by shifting focus to the therapist's personal experiences when discussing his own burnout.
Invokes loyalty and shared identity (veteran status) as a barrier when the therapist suggests practical steps like job-searching.
(inferred) Minimizes his own needs (benefits for kids) by emphasizing emotional obligation, resisting concrete action.

ambivalence.for_change: I feel I could get my kids health insurance if I switched jobs.
ambivalence.against_change: I feel like I would be fucking over the whole nation turning my back on another veteran.

values_and_stakes: His relationship with his boss, framed as family-like due to shared veteran identity.
His self-image as a loyal person who doesn't abandon 'family'.
(inferred) His role as a provider securing benefits for his three children.
key_facts: He is currently on the honor roll in his master's degree program.
He has three children and no benefits at his current job.
His boss is 72 years old and a fellow veteran.

background: (inferred) A young adult in a romantic relationship, likely active on social media and with a social circle including friends and a best friend of the ex-partner.
self_view_of_problem: My boyfriend broke up with me without explanation, which is cruel and irrational, and the resulting anxiety is preventing me from eating or sleeping.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from internal distress by focusing on the ex-partner's irrationality and cruelty.
Uses humor and fatalistic acceptance ('haha') to minimize the depth of her own pain when discussing coping strategies.
(inferred) Clings to the hope of reconciliation as a way to avoid fully confronting the finality of the breakup.

ambivalence.for_change: She admits the anxiety is 'killing me' and she doesn't know how to handle it, showing a pull toward seeking relief.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Letting go of the hope for reconciliation feels like accepting a profound loss and the injustice of his unexplained cruelty.

values_and_stakes: The specific relationship with her ex-boyfriend, which she hopes to restore.
Her self-image as a reasonable person wronged by an irrational partner.
(inferred) Her standing within her friend group, as she does not want to 'bother my friends too much' with her distress.
key_facts: The ex-boyfriend broke up via a Facebook story and refuses all communication, including reading messages without responding.
She has already enlisted the ex's best friend to mediate, but the ex pretended nothing was wrong.
She reports physical symptoms of distress: 'I can't eat or sleep.'

background: (inferred) A young adult in a relationship, living independently or with family during a pandemic lockdown, with no children currently.
self_view_of_problem: I feel depressed because of the lockdown; it's making me depressed, and I'm bored and sick on top of everything.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from personal problem to asking the therapist about their coping strategies (e.g., 'So how are you coping?', 'Do you draw?').
Minimizes the severity of the problem by reframing constraints as 'not a bad thing' (e.g., 'That's not a bad thing though').
(inferred) Avoids deeper exploration of depression by quickly pivoting to casual, hobby-related topics (e.g., gaming, movies).

ambivalence.for_change: I hate being this way and want to start a life with my boyfriend, which I can't do right now.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Feels an emotional pull toward the comfort and safety of familiar, low-effort digital routines (gaming, YouTube) that provide immediate distraction from depression.

values_and_stakes: The relationship with her boyfriend and the shared goal of starting a life together.
Online social connections with friends through gaming and hanging out (e.g., Among Us).
(inferred) Her identity as a fun, easygoing person who values positive memories over dwelling on problems.
key_facts: She is currently sick with a cold, which compounds her depressive feelings.
She primarily copes by watching YouTube and playing RPG games on her phone or PC.
She explicitly states she is starting to feel better by the end of the session after talking.

background: She is a single mother of three children (an 8-year-old daughter and 5-year-old twin boys), working full-time while pursuing a master's degree with student loans.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as being overwhelmed by an immediate academic deadline (a 10-page paper due at 1 a.m. tomorrow) while juggling full-time work and single parenting, all while trying to set a good example after her husband's death.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Immediately focuses on logistical obstacles (like family being far away or used PTO) when practical solutions are suggested, rather than engaging with the solution's feasibility.

(inferred) Minimizes her own capacity for help-seeking (e.g., 'i guess i could ask my neighbor') and resorts to self-reliant, minimal workarounds (like having her daughter make sandwiches) before considering external support.

ambivalence.for_change: She acknowledges feeling overwhelmed and seeks help to make a plan, showing a pull toward gaining control and meeting her responsibilities.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) An emotional pull toward maintaining total self-reliance and not burdening others, rooted in her identity as a capable single mother managing everything alone.

values_and_stakes: Being a good example and provider for her children following her husband's death.
Her academic and career advancement through her master's degree, which involves student loans.
Maintaining her full-time job and income, as she has no child support and needs extra money (e.g., from MTurk).
key_facts: She has only written 2 pages of a 10-page paper due at 1 a.m. tomorrow.
She works from 6 a.m. to 5 p.m. today and then must feed her kids and handle their bedtime routines.
She has already used her paid time off for digital learning days and must bring her children to work with her next week.

background: (inferred) The client is unemployed, actively searching for a job, and is in a long-distance romantic relationship with someone from their past who is also facing financial hardship.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as needing money but only finding jobs with hours that cause anxiety about walking home late, compounded by stress from their partner's financial struggles and the emotional difficulty of the long-distance separation.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from deeper emotional exploration by focusing on practical logistics (e.g., shifts from relationship stress to transportation solutions).
Minimizes personal strain when directly asked about the burden of helping their partner, insisting they would give more if they could.

ambivalence.for_change: The client wants to regain financial independence and have 'my own stuff again' to reduce personal anxiety and reliance on online surveys.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The client is emotionally attached to the role of being their partner's primary supporter, fearing that reducing this support would threaten their identity as the one person 'in his corner.'

values_and_stakes: The long-distance romantic relationship with a childhood friend, which provides emotional connection but is strained by distance and financial stress.
Personal safety and financial stability, both at risk if they take a late-night job without a secure ride home.
The role as their partner's essential financial and emotional supporter, which they risk losing if they prioritize their own needs exclusively.
key_facts: The client has already helped their partner financially a lot but is now 'at my end too' financially.
The client just visited their partner's apartment this past weekend and has been upset since leaving.
The partner is unemployed due to COVID-19 and relying on unemployment assistance while job searching.

background: (inferred) An unemployed individual living alone, who lost their job due to pandemic-related cuts.
self_view_of_problem: I am depressed, there is no hope, and I am struggling with the pandemic and loneliness, feeling extremely isolated and stuck at home.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions by citing emotional incapacity (e.g., 'don't know if i will have the energy to do it').
Expresses self-defeating beliefs that undermine initiative (e.g., 'I don't feel qualified').

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) A desire to feel better and less isolated, acknowledging the therapist's suggestions are a 'great idea'.
ambivalence.against_change: A fear that attempting change will expose inadequacy or confirm a self-view as a failure, draining limited energy.

values_and_stakes: (inferred) The safety and familiarity of staying in bed, which provides a retreat from overwhelming stress.
(inferred) The identity of someone who is trying, which could be threatened by actual failure in a new job search.
key_facts: The client lost their job due to pandemic cuts, though they did not like it.
The client lives alone and reports having no one to talk to.
The client spends a lot of time in bed worrying about life and crying.

background: (inferred) A person with a social circle of friends, likely a student or young adult given the focus on peer trust and free time for reading.
self_view_of_problem: My friends hide important matters from me and avoid me, which creates depression on my mind and stops me from concentrating on any other works.
resistance_drivers: Rejects therapist's reframing that shifts blame away from friends (e.g., suggesting friends might feel uncomfortable).
Redirects from discussing specific interpersonal dynamics to asking for general, impersonal solutions for depression and stress.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to stop feeling depressed and unable to concentrate, so I am seeking help.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Changing my view might mean accepting that my friends' actions are not a pure betrayal, which threatens my identity as a blindly trusting and wronged person.

values_and_stakes: The specific friendships where I feel betrayed and ignored.
My self-image as a very trusting and friendly person.
(inferred) My ability to concentrate on and perform other works or responsibilities.
key_facts: The client has already tried to talk to their friends about the issue and they did not respond.
The client reports that the situation causes depression and an inability to concentrate on other work.
The client likes to read books and is considering using that to cope.

background: (inferred) The client is a friend of a woman with a drinking problem, likely a peer in a social circle, concerned about the friend's behavior and its impact on family.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as trying to help a friend who is a drunk and denies it, which has backfired because the friend is now spreading lies and cutting off contact.
resistance_drivers: Seeks immediate, actionable solutions from the therapist when feeling helpless (e.g., 'like what for example, talking does not work? so call the cops on her?')
Considers withdrawing entirely when interventions seem futile (e.g., 'or should I just step back and let it be if even her husband does not care?')

ambivalence.for_change: The client feels a moral duty to intervene to prevent harm, especially the risk of the friend losing custody of her child.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The client fears that further action will escalate conflict and damage her own reputation and relationships, as the friend is already spreading lies.

values_and_stakes: The friendship itself, which is now severed (blocked on social media, no communication).
The client's own reputation, as the friend is spreading lies about her being a terrible person trying to cause trouble.
The well-being of the friend's child, who is at risk of custody loss if the drinking continues.
key_facts: The friend gets drunk and mean, falling off chairs in bars at least 3-4 times a week.
The friend's husband does not confront her about her drinking, which the client sees as due to verbal abuse.
The friend has blocked the client on social media and is not talking to her anymore.

background: (inferred) The client is an adult living alone, likely unemployed or working from home, with no current social support network.
self_view_of_problem: I feel very lonely and depressed, have no friends or family by my side, and see no point to live.
resistance_drivers: Deflects positive suggestions by contrasting their own perceived emptiness with others' coping (e.g., 'You must be a lucky person. I do not see anything in myself').
Expresses helplessness and inability to generate solutions when given advice (e.g., 'It is so hard to think of something when you are locked home').

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) A desire to feel less lonely and find a point to living, evidenced by seeking conversation and planning small activities like candles and music.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear that engaging with emotions (like crying) confirms a core identity of being a failure, which reinforces withdrawal.

values_and_stakes: (inferred) The safety of isolation — avoiding the risk of further disappointment or rejection by not reaching out to others.
(inferred) A self-concept as a 'failure' — changing would require dismantling this entrenched self-view, which currently organizes their experience.
key_facts: The client has started drinking recently.
The client used to enjoy reading but now just stares at the TV without realizing what is on.
The client plans to look for candles and try to read like in old times this evening.

background: (inferred) A person who has been single since a breakup four years ago, currently volunteers and maintains an awkward friendship with their ex-partner.
self_view_of_problem: I have a strange complex where I need to feel needed, which I never discovered until recently, and it makes me feel depressed even though the breakup was four years ago.
resistance_drivers: Corrects the therapist's interpretation when it mischaracterizes their feelings (e.g., denies losing interest, clarifies volunteering vs. talking to ex).
Minimizes the emotional impact of current circumstances (e.g., describes feeling 'a little down' and an 'awkward' friendship that doesn't involve much talk).

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to understand and overcome this 'strange complex' that causes my depression.
ambivalence.against_change: My identity is tied to being needed and helpful, so changing risks losing that core sense of purpose.

values_and_stakes: The friendship with my ex-partner, even though it's awkward and we rarely talk.
The role of being a helper, which provides satisfaction through activities like volunteering.
key_facts: The client's only romantic relationship ended four years ago, and they have not had another since.
The client discovered they have a 'strange complex' of needing to feel needed only recently.
The client enjoys volunteering and finds satisfaction in helping others.

background: (inferred) Spike is an unemployed individual who lives in a rural area and is attempting to earn income through online platforms like MTurk and YouTube.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as a financial crisis and a crisis of self-confidence stemming from unemployment and health-related limitations.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Deflects by shifting focus to the therapist's situation when suggestions are made about his own behavior.
(inferred) Minimizes engagement with suggested activities by framing them as chores or admitting he hasn't done them for days/weeks.

ambivalence.for_change: He expresses a desire to stay encouraged and acknowledges that getting outside might help.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is emotionally attached to staying indoors due to a combination of health fear and low motivation.

values_and_stakes: His physical health and safety from Covid-19.
His financial independence and ability to earn income.
(inferred) His sense of autonomy and control over his work environment.
key_facts: He lost his job in January.
He has health conditions that make Covid-19 very risky for him.
He has not sat on his porch for days or taken a walk for weeks.

background: A university student taking two online courses, living at home and experiencing social isolation due to the pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as being 'just a little behind' due to the pandemic disrupting normal routines and making life patterns aimless, leading to procrastination and being 'lazy'.
resistance_drivers: Corrects the therapist's interpretation to maintain control over the narrative of their situation (e.g., clarifying 'taking a break' was just for the session, not from school).
Minimizes the severity of the problem by using qualifiers like 'just' and stating they are 'doing fine so far'.
(inferred) Deflects focus from their own struggles by shifting attention to the therapist's well-being and academic performance.

ambivalence.for_change: They admit to feeling disappointed in not being their 'best self' and have been trying the therapist's suggested tactic more often this week.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is an emotional attachment to the identity of being 'usually very conscientious,' making current 'lazy' behavior a protected, temporary state that excuses full accountability.

values_and_stakes: Their self-image as a mature, hard-working, and conscientious student.
The successful completion of their two university courses and exams.
(inferred) Maintaining a sense of control and normalcy in their daily routines and life patterns.
key_facts: The client has an exam and an assignment due at the end of the month, and another set due at the end of next month.
The client states they have been trying the therapist's suggested tactic more often this week.
The client plans to 'sleep late for awhile' to persevere and complete their work.

background: (inferred) The client is an individual with a social circle of friends, likely living in a context where COVID-19 is a concern, and is actively trying to maintain social connections.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as friends excluding them from social gatherings, using COVID as an excuse, which makes them feel bitter, sad, and doubtful about the friendships.
resistance_drivers: Shifts to self-blame or internalization when therapist suggests giving friends another chance (e.g., 'I really thought we were better than this but I guess not').
Deflects actionable advice by retreating to passive observation (e.g., 'Im going to do observing of myself and think so over').

ambivalence.for_change: The client admits a desire to bring new people into their life, indicating a pull toward expanding their social circle.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The client fears that confronting the exclusion or moving on from these friends would mean accepting a painful loss of existing social bonds and shared history.

values_and_stakes: The specific friendships with the group that went to lunch without them.
(inferred) Their role and sense of belonging within that established friend circle.
(inferred) The emotional security and reliability they derive from these long-term connections.
key_facts: The client called multiple friends to have lunch and everyone said no due to COVID.
The client later learned that all those friends were out together for lunch without including them.
A friend told the client they were excluded because the group thought the client was busy and couldn't attend.

background: (inferred) A married woman with children, part of a close-knit social circle of couples and families.
self_view_of_problem: My friend is making a destructive and erratic decision by leaving her husband to be with a woman, which has thrown me for a loop and upset our entire friend group.
resistance_drivers: Dismisses or deflects direct challenges to her judgment of the friend's actions (e.g., when therapist suggests the friend might not realize the impact).
Resists suggestions to end the friendship despite agreeing it's tough, indicating an attachment or obligation that conflicts with her stated disapproval.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I feel a pull to protect my family's stability and my own moral framework from the disruption caused by my friend's choices.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I feel a pull away from severing the friendship because it would mean losing a long-standing relationship and fracturing my social circle, which is a source of identity and support.

values_and_stakes: The stability and cohesion of her family unit and her role as a wife and mother within it.
Her long-standing friendship and the shared social network of couples and children.
Her moral standing and role as the 'patient' one within the upset friend group.
key_facts: The client's friend is leaving her husband to pursue a relationship with a woman.
The client, her husband, their children, and the friend's husband are all part of an interconnected social circle.
The client has already spoken to her friend about her feelings and found her friend to be dismissive.

background: (inferred) A woman who lost her job due to COVID-19, contracted COVID leading to health issues, and is currently financially dependent on her partner while living at home.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as needing to 'overcome from body shaming' caused by weight gain after job loss, and as feeling 'literally nothing' due to having 'no job, no body structure, no boy friend' and facing teasing and a lack of support.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from action plans by immediately raising practical or emotional obstacles (e.g., mentions distance to park, fear of teasing when going out is suggested).
Uses physical and emotional suffering (health issues, feeling hurt by comments) as a reason for inaction when behavioral change is encouraged.

ambivalence.for_change: She acknowledges suggestions are good ideas and expresses a wish to 'start one by one' to feel better and gain happiness.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A deep-seated fear that changing her behavior (going out, exercising) will expose her to the painful shame and teasing she associates with her current body and situation.

values_and_stakes: Financial security and shelter, as she depends on her partner for rent and has no income.
(inferred) The existing relationship with her partner, which provides material support despite the 'non sense' and lack of understanding she endures.
A sense of safety and avoidance of immediate emotional pain, which staying at home currently provides.
key_facts: She has a library card but had forgotten about it until the therapist mentioned it.
She states she will go to the park even though it is far, by walk.
She got COVID, which infected her lungs and causes daily migraines, impacting her health.

background: (inferred) A person who is unemployed and living alone in an apartment, with mother and sister living nearby.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is the anxiety of being trapped in the apartment due to the pandemic, compounded by recent grief from losing multiple family members, including an uncle just days ago.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Minimizes current distress by immediately pivoting to positive coping strategies when asked about their state.
(inferred) Deflects from exploring the emotional impact of recent losses by focusing on practical daily routines.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) They want relief from the anxiety and isolation of being trapped and the weight of cumulative grief.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is a pull to avoid fully confronting the depth of their grief and the vulnerabilities linked to their past substance use and job loss.

values_and_stakes: The stability and routine provided by daily activities like exercise, cooking, and video games.
The proximity and regular contact with mother and sister.
(inferred) A self-image of being someone who handles difficulties and 'does the best they can'.
key_facts: The client has lost six family members in the past year, including an uncle a couple of days ago.
The client dealt with heavy drinking and drug use problems at the beginning of the pandemic.
The client lost their job, leading to financial woes at the start of the pandemic.

background: (inferred) A woman in her late 20s or early 30s who was in a 5-year relationship that recently ended, and who has a small family.
self_view_of_problem: I'm having a hard time because my boyfriend and I just broke up, and I'm nervous with the holidays coming up that I will be sad to be alone.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Seeks validation for the breakup decision rather than exploring deeper emotional conflict.
(inferred) Shifts focus from present pain to future-oriented self-improvement platitudes when sadness is mentioned.

ambivalence.for_change: I broke it off because his political support for Trump became overwhelming and we weren't right for each other.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The attachment and identity formed over 5 years makes the fresh hurt and fear of being alone during the holidays a powerful pull back toward the relationship's comfort.

values_and_stakes: A 5-year romantic partnership and the shared history and routine it provided.
The emotional security and companionship during holidays and other traditionally shared times.
(inferred) A coherent self-narrative as someone in a stable, long-term relationship.
key_facts: The client initiated the breakup due to overwhelming disagreement with her boyfriend's political views, specifically his support for Trump.
The breakup is very recent and feels fresh and painful to the client.
The client has a plan to be with her small family for the holidays.

background: Works in healthcare for a large company, facing high workload expectations and insufficient support from corporate.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is that corporate sets unreasonable goals with a lack of support, causing my work performance to suffer and making me feel overwhelmed and unorganized.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from internal coping to external solutions when therapist suggests personal strategies (e.g., asking for therapist's ideas instead of exploring own capacity).
Expresses past frustration with organizational responsiveness, implying a belief that raising concerns is futile.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to find ways to cope and improve my work performance because the stress is overwhelming.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I am attached to the belief that the problem is entirely external (corporate expectations and lack of support), which protects me from examining my own role or limitations.

values_and_stakes: My job performance and professional competence are at risk if I cannot meet expectations.
My sense of safety and quality in healthcare delivery is threatened by unrealistic corporate goals.
(inferred) My professional identity as a capable healthcare worker is at stake if I admit I cannot handle the workload.
key_facts: The client has previously raised workload concerns with the organization and was not given a solution, only asked for their own ideas.
The client works for a big company where corporate sets goals they view as unreasonably high and unsafe given time and support constraints.
The client feels their work performance is suffering due to being too busy and unorganized.

background: (inferred) A sales professional whose contract is ending this month and is being let go due to department downsizing.
self_view_of_problem: I am very anxious about finding another job during the pandemic, worried about job vacancies being few and far between, and somewhat afraid of failing due to financial commitments.
resistance_drivers: Shifts to practical obstacles when offered general encouragement (e.g., asks for specific ideas when told to search online or get help from friends).
Qualifies optimistic statements with concrete fears (e.g., agrees to try harder but immediately cites financial commitments).

ambivalence.for_change: I should never give up and I need to pull my socks up, believing hard work will pay.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear that effort may not overcome external market conditions and financial pressure, creating a pull toward protective pessimism.

values_and_stakes: Financial stability and meeting financial commitments.
(inferred) Professional identity and self-view as a competent salesperson.
(inferred) Social standing and self-reliance, as suggested by hesitance to rely on friends for practical help.
key_facts: The client's job contract ends this month and is not being renewed due to department downsizing.
The client has already started preparing a resume.
The client reports that only very few of their friends are in the sales field.

background: (inferred) A person recently out of a romantic relationship, likely navigating social circles that include the ex-partner and a former friend.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is a past event: a boyfriend who cheated with a friend and lied, which initially caused anger, but that stage has passed.
resistance_drivers: Uses minimization and past-tense framing ('stage passed', 'totally ok') when the therapist suggests emotional processing or future impact.
Agrees superficially ('I guess', 'Yea i know right', 'Certainly did') without elaborating on personal feelings, deflecting deeper exploration.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) A desire to move forward and be happy, looking forward to better future relationships.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) An attachment to a self-image of strength and positivity that avoids dwelling on negative emotions like anger or betrayal.

values_and_stakes: A self-concept as a 'strong person' who handles things well and doesn't dwell.
The social identity and peace of mind maintained by not processing the anger and betrayal deeply.
(inferred) Future relationships that might be jeopardized if unresolved trust issues from this betrayal are not addressed.
key_facts: The client initiated the breakup due to the boyfriend's cheating with a friend and persistent lying.
The client has not really spoken to anyone else about this event.
The client reports the initial anger has passed and they are choosing to be happy and look forward.

background: A person in a COVID-19 quarantine situation, married with grandchildren, currently isolated from family and friends. (inferred) He is likely older and retired or of grandparent age.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as 'pandemic depression' caused by complete isolation from loved ones and compounded by his wife's extreme paranoia about the virus, which leads to her sanitizing excessively and 'bitching' at him.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from his own emotional state to external problems (like his wife's behavior) when asked how he is coping.
Seeks concrete, immediate solutions from the therapist ('Any thoughts on calming her down?') rather than exploring his own feelings or adaptive strategies.
(inferred) Minimizes his own distress by framing it as a situational problem with an external cause ('It's been going on for months with no end in sight'), which may resist internal exploration.

ambivalence.for_change: He admits to feeling depressed and isolated and seeks help on how to 'deal with it,' indicating a desire for relief from his distress.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He may be attached to viewing the problem as entirely external (the pandemic, his wife's paranoia), which protects him from examining his own potential contributions to the conflict or his emotional coping deficits.

values_and_stakes: His relationship with his wife is at risk if her paranoia and the resulting conflict continue unchecked.
His connections with his grandchildren and extended family are at risk due to the physical isolation.
(inferred) His sense of autonomy and peace at home is at risk due to his wife's controlling sanitization behaviors and complaints.
key_facts: He has been in complete isolation from family and friends for months.
He states video chats with family are 'not the same' as physical contact.
His wife sanitizes the house excessively and 'bitches at him,' which he identifies as a major stressor.

background: A person whose five-year engagement has ended, currently staying with a friend and needing to find a new apartment. (inferred) They are navigating a major life transition during the pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: They frame the problem as 'starting over again' after a long-term relationship ends, feeling nervous and apprehensive about the process.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Minimizes or deflects emotional depth by quickly agreeing with therapist suggestions and pivoting to practical tasks.
(inferred) Avoids exploring painful emotions by focusing on logistical next steps like moving and hobbies when emotional topics arise.

ambivalence.for_change: They acknowledge potential benefits, stating 'I will have time to focus on myself and start anew.'
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) They are attached to the security and identity of the long-term relationship, making the prospect of being alone feel like a loss of a familiar life.

values_and_stakes: The stability and shared future represented by the five-year engagement.
Their current living stability and support from the friend they are staying with.
(inferred) Their sense of adult independence and competence tied to having their own home and established life.
key_facts: The client's engagement of over five years has ended.
The client is currently staying with a friend and needs to find a new apartment.
The client believes the pandemic had an impact on their relationship.

background: (inferred) The client is married and socializes as part of a couple, but lacks distinct personal hobbies or a strong sense of self outside of these roles.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as a lifelong pattern where 'every person I become friends with uses me and throws me away when they're done,' and sometimes wonders if 'it must be me' or if they are 'annoying,' despite seeing themselves as friendly, assertive, outspoken, and kind.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from self-examination by externalizing blame onto others' character ('They use me,' 'Who even has the nerve to blatantly use somebody like that?').
Resorts to fatalistic acceptance when patterns persist ('that's just the way the cards were dealt'), shutting down exploration of alternative causes or solutions.
(inferred) Minimizes their own role in relational dynamics by emphasizing their positive traits ('I don't LET people walk all over me') while overlooking possible passive or enabling behaviors.

ambivalence.for_change: They desire to 'meet people and form actual friendships' and feel hopeful when presented with a concrete strategy like finding common interests.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is a protective pull away from change because examining their own role threatens a self-image of being a kind, assertive person who is simply unlucky, and risks admitting complicity in the pattern.

values_and_stakes: The existing, albeit unsatisfying, friendships that provide some social contact and a defined role (as a giver of money or emotional support).
The marital social dynamic and joint friendships as a couple, which could be disrupted if she changes her relational patterns.
(inferred) Their self-concept as a morally superior, wronged party, which would be compromised if they acknowledged their own contributions to the dynamic.
key_facts: The client has a history of cutting contact completely after finally expressing their feelings to a friend.
The client is currently holding in their feelings and barely responding to friends, waiting for them to ask for money or dump problems to then 'say my peace.'
The client recently told a friend she had no money, and that friend has not contacted her since.

background: (inferred) A woman with a long-term female friend who recently had a baby, navigating a strained friendship within a limited social circle.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is a friend who 'picks a fight with me and others in a bid to quarrel and feel entitled,' acting 'very disgusting' and 'like a child,' which forces me to tolerate 'bad attitude' and 'manage the Nonsense.'
resistance_drivers: Deflects direct questions about her own feelings or actions by refocusing on the friend's behavior (e.g., when asked if something is bothering her or how to handle it, she details the friend's actions instead).
Expresses disgust and moral judgment ('disgusting,' 'childish') when the therapist suggests empathy or an opening for reconciliation, framing the friend as unworthy of engagement.
(inferred) Minimizes her own emotional investment ('I'm indifferent,' 'bare think about her') when confronted with the loss of a long-term friendship, suggesting a protective downplaying of hurt.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) She feels a pull to resolve the tension, as evidenced by sending a birthday message as 'the least I can do' and initially being worried about the friend's silence.
ambivalence.against_change: She is pulled away from change by a strong sense of disgust and moral superiority, viewing reconciliation as tolerating childish, entitled behavior from someone who should 'behave better.'

values_and_stakes: A 15-year friendship that represents a significant history and investment, which she would lose by fully letting go.
Her self-image as someone with a limited, carefully managed social circle ('I limit my circle'), where losing a member disrupts her chosen structure.
(inferred) Her sense of personal dignity and boundaries, which she believes would be compromised by 'crawling' to apologize or actively seeking reconciliation.
key_facts: She sent her friend a birthday message recently, indicating a residual gesture of connection despite her stated indifference.
The friend stopped responding to her in the last month of pregnancy, and there has been 'no word' for months since the baby's birth.
She describes the friend as recalling incidents from five years ago during conflicts, indicating a pattern of bringing up old grievances.

background: (inferred) An adult with a long-term friendship network, likely employed and socially active, who is navigating a conflict with a close friend of over 20 years.
self_view_of_problem: My friend is embarrassing himself on Facebook by spouting extreme talking points he never cared about before, and he's pulling me into arguments while refusing to listen to reason.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from his own emotional reaction to analyzing the friend's motives (e.g., speculating the friend is 'lashing out' due to something he's dealing with).

Seeks external validation and solutions from the therapist rather than exploring his own role or feelings in the conflict (e.g., repeatedly asks 'Not sure what to do?' and for the therapist's personal experiences).

ambivalence.for_change: He wants the friend's embarrassing and extreme online behavior to stop because it is damaging the friend's reputation and straining their friendship.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He fears that directly confronting the friend might overwhelm him or damage the long-term friendship, creating a sense of vulnerability and loss.

values_and_stakes: His 20-year close friendship with this individual.
The shared social reputation and harmony within their friend group.
His own comfort and desire to avoid frustrating, eye-rolling interactions.
key_facts: The client's friend has recently started posting extreme political views on Facebook after showing no prior interest.
The friend tries to pull the client into arguments with other friends online.
Other mutual friends share the client's frustration with the friend's behavior.

background: Works full-time for a large corporation, has a family, and feels trapped in his current career path.
self_view_of_problem: I feel trapped in a meaningless corporate job that bores and drains me, and I'm fearful that trying something new will jeopardize my financial stability.
resistance_drivers: Expresses fear of financial insecurity when considering a career change.
Highlights practical constraints like lack of time due to family and full-time job as a barrier to taking action.
Seeks external validation for the feasibility of change (e.g., 'Do you think it's even possible?').

ambivalence.for_change: I need to do something about this because I think it's starting to affect my mental health!
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I am attached to the security and familiarity of my current corporate job, even though it feels meaningless.

values_and_stakes: Financial stability and ability to support himself.
Time and energy for his family.
(inferred) Professional identity and competence built within the corporate environment.
key_facts: The client has only ever worked in big corporate environments.
The client feels his work is part of a meaningless machine where his efforts lack meaningful outcomes.
The client is considering starting a side project while still employed to explore new options.
