background: (inferred) A college-educated adult living with their parents, currently working an unstable online job while seeking stable employment.
self_view_of_problem: I won't ever get a proper job and move out of my parents' home because I submit hundreds of applications and don't get responses, and the jobs I want require experience I can't get.
resistance_drivers: Shifts to externalizing blame when faced with the difficulty of the job market (e.g., citing lack of responses and experience requirements).
Acquiesces to therapist's reassurance and reframes the problem as a matter of timing or personal readiness, which avoids deeper exploration of action.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I feel stressed and frustrated by my unstable situation and want the independence and stability of a 'normal adult job.'
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Changing my approach or lowering my standards feels like a threat to my identity as a college graduate who deserves better than retail.

values_and_stakes: Financial independence and the ability to move out of my parents' home.
A professional identity aligned with my college education, not a retail job.
A stable, 'proper' job in a field of interest like museums or animal work.
key_facts: The client has submitted hundreds of job applications with minimal response.
The client currently works an online job they describe as unstable but more lucrative than retail.
The client volunteers once a week with animals.

background: (inferred) A young adult living in a small town, recently single and navigating social dynamics.
self_view_of_problem: She sees the problem as regretting her decision to break up with her boyfriend for someone else and now wanting him back, but he is angry and doesn't want her back.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus from self-reflection to external tactics (e.g., how to get him back) when therapist questions her underlying motives.
Deflects by externalizing blame onto his friends' dislike or his temper when therapist suggests a softer, introspective approach.

ambivalence.for_change: She admits she might have liked the title of being with the popular guy more than the person himself.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She fears losing the social status and attention that came with being his girlfriend.

values_and_stakes: Her social status and popularity in the small town.
The relationship with her ex-boyfriend, which provided external validation.
(inferred) Approval from her peer group, as her friends previously validated her by saying she could do better.
key_facts: She broke up with him because she liked another person, who was the popular and cutest guy in town.
She has been secretly watching his social media and sees other girls asking him out.
All of his friends hate her now, leaving her with no allies in his social circle.

background: (inferred) The client is an individual who was in a long-distance relationship that ended abruptly around Thanksgiving last year, with communication occurring solely via phone, text, and email.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as their boyfriend changing over time, losing interest, and moving on, which has left them feeling very sad, especially around the holidays.
resistance_drivers: Shifts focus to the therapist's experience when discussing their own emotional pain (e.g., asking about the therapist's breakup).
Accepts the situation as final without exploring alternatives (e.g., 'I just accepted it as he just moved on, and I had to do the same').

(inferred) Minimizes the depth of the relationship when describing its nature (e.g., noting it was only communication-based and 'kind of weird'), potentially to preempt judgment or deeper emotional exploration.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) The client seeks emotional support by initiating the conversation, indicating a desire to process the sadness and not feel alone in it.
ambivalence.against_change: The client is attached to the narrative that the relationship is definitively over and that moving on is the only option, which protects them from the uncertainty and potential rejection of re-engagement.

values_and_stakes: The emotional safety and validation found in the long-distance connection, which they describe as 'hard to love from a distance'.
(inferred) Their self-concept as someone who handles loss with acceptance and independence, avoiding perceived neediness.
(inferred) The hope for closure or reassurance about the ex-partner's well-being, as they express concern over not knowing 'whether or not he is safe or anything'.
key_facts: The client has attempted to contact the ex-partner via call, text, and email with no response since around Thanksgiving last year.
The relationship was entirely long-distance and conducted only through phone, text, and email, with no in-person meetings.
The client has no access to the ex-partner's friends, family, or social media, indicating complete isolation from his social context.

background: A divorced mother of three children (6-year-old twin boys and an 8-year-old daughter), working a job that starts at 6 AM, and currently pursuing a master's degree about halfway to completion.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as being 'so tired all the time' and feeling like 'everything i do just isnt enough' due to the overwhelming demands of work, kids, and school.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by asking the therapist personal questions about their family and credentials when discussing her stress.
Responds with sarcasm or dismissal ('I WISH I HAD TIME LOL') when given generic self-care suggestions like mindfulness or meditation.
(inferred) Minimizes her own achievements and deflects praise ('i guess') when the therapist affirms her, suggesting resistance to internalizing positive feedback.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) She desires relief from her constant exhaustion and the feeling of inadequacy, as shown by her seeking suggestions and saying 'i guess it is worth a try'.
ambivalence.against_change: She is attached to her identity as a 'multitasking queen' and the packed schedule that defines her current life, making the idea of slowing down or restructuring her time feel like a threat to that role.

values_and_stakes: Her role as a reliable mother who manages to get off work to meet her children after school.
Her career advancement and investment represented by completing her master's degree.
(inferred) Her sense of competence and achievement derived from managing her demanding work-family-school balance.
key_facts: She starts work at 6 AM to finish by 2 PM so she can get her children off the bus at 3 PM.
She is about halfway through completing her master's degree.
She describes her children as 'easier to talk to than my kids LOL' and 'not as annoying', indicating a strained or fatigued dynamic in her primary relationship.

background: A married person whose husband has been battling an illness for weeks, causing significant life stress. (inferred) They are actively seeking coping strategies for anxiety.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as feeling anxious lately, which they connect to their husband's illness, stating 'I think as he feels better I will too.'
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Seeks external advice and solutions rather than exploring internal emotional states, repeatedly asking 'Do you have any ideas?' or 'Any other advice?'
(inferred) Deflects from deeper exploration of the anxiety's root causes by focusing on practical coping tips, like asking about diet and calling friends after the therapist probes for triggers.

ambivalence.for_change: They acknowledge feeling anxious and seek help to feel better, indicating a desire for relief.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is an emotional pull to maintain vigilance and worry as a form of connection and care for their sick husband, making full relaxation feel like a neglect of duty.

values_and_stakes: The health and well-being of her sick husband is a primary concrete relationship at stake.
(inferred) Her role as a caregiver and supportive partner, which could feel diminished if her anxiety resolves independently of her husband's recovery.
(inferred) Her personal sanity and ability to function, which is at risk if the stress of caregiving continues unmanaged.
key_facts: Her husband has been battling an illness for weeks, a primary stressor she explicitly links to her anxiety.
She has been experiencing anxiety for about a month, correlating with the duration of her husband's illness.
She reports that her husband finally has some medicine that is starting to help, indicating a potential shift in the situation.

background: She is a mother of three boys and works a full-time job. Her husband was recently laid off and does not contribute financially.
self_view_of_problem: She feels everyone hates her, that people are only nice as a favor, and that no one cares about her or understands her feelings.
resistance_drivers: Withdraws and avoids social contact when feeling depressed or misunderstood
Dismisses potential sources of support by framing them as burdensome or unavailable
(inferred) Minimizes her own needs and prioritizes caretaking of others, blocking self-care

ambivalence.for_change: She acknowledges she needs to start focusing more on herself and quit trying to please everyone else.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Changing would threaten her identity as a self-sacrificing mother and sole provider, a role that defines her worth.

values_and_stakes: Her role as a reliable mother to her three boys
Her relationship with her ailing mother, whom she protects from her problems
(inferred) Her identity as the family's sole financial and emotional provider
key_facts: She has stopped talking to her friends and keeps to herself.
When depressed, she cannot summon the energy to exercise despite previous attempts.
After work, she goes home and lies on the couch for the rest of the day.

background: (inferred) A married individual working in a job with reduced hours due to the coronavirus pandemic, living in a rural area. Their husband is self-employed and was recently sick and unable to work.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is that reduced work hours and a smaller paycheck, combined with their husband's past illness and lack of income, create overwhelming stress because they cannot pay all the bills and eat, and they cannot get outside help because they make too much money to qualify.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Immediately cites practical obstacles (like rural location, driving times, and gas costs) when the therapist suggests actionable solutions like finding another job.
(inferred) Presents their situation as an unresolvable totality ('I am at my end') when asked for a plan, shutting down problem-solving.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) They want relief from the overwhelming stress and financial pressure of not being able to pay bills and eat.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is a pull toward exhaustion and hopelessness, where the effort to seek new solutions feels futile and more burdensome.

values_and_stakes: Financial stability and the ability to pay bills, eat, and cover hospital expenses.
(inferred) The stability and well-being of their marital household, which is under strain from dual income loss.
(inferred) Their sense of self-reliance and not needing outside help, which is challenged by their ineligibility for assistance.
key_facts: The client's paycheck is quite smaller due to reduced hours.
The client's husband is self-employed and had no income whatsoever during his illness.
The client lives in a rural area, which complicates finding additional work due to driving times and gas costs.

background: A 26-year-old college student who has been living away from her parents for college, is in a relationship, and is the favorite child of her parents.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as her parents not understanding who she is, forcing their traditional beliefs on her, and guilt-tripping her over her desire to go on a trip with her boyfriend.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by focusing on external validation (e.g., noting her boyfriend's parents are 'totally cool') when her own actions conflict with parental expectations.
Expresses confusion and anxiety as a barrier to asserting her own voice, rooted in a lifelong pattern of being monitored and bullied by her parents.
(inferred) Minimizes the severity of potential consequences (e.g., 'worst case I won't talk to them for a while') to avoid confronting the full emotional weight of defying her parents.

ambivalence.for_change: She desires autonomy and the freedom to live according to her own beliefs, as seen in her frustration with her parents' restrictions and her independent life at college.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She fears losing her identity as the 'favorite child' and the emotional security that comes with her parents' approval, making direct confrontation feel threatening.

values_and_stakes: Her relationship with her parents, especially her favored status within the family.
Her personal autonomy and ability to make independent life choices without guilt or monitoring.
Her romantic relationship and the freedom to share experiences like trips with her boyfriend.
key_facts: She is 26 years old and has been living away from her parents for college.
She has been engaging in behaviors that directly contradict her parents' traditional beliefs without their knowledge.
Her parents have explicitly stated that going on the trip would be disrespecting them and the entire family.

background: Works in sales at a manufacturing business, a job that has become unfulfilling due to reduced workload during the coronavirus pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: I've been having anxiety issues because my job is unfulfilling and I think I can do more, and I have turned impatient which in turn gives me anxiety issues.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Hesitates to take direct action (like asking for more work) due to fear of social judgment or appearing 'weird'.
(inferred) Feels a sense of obligation or being depended on by the company, which creates inertia against seeking change.

ambivalence.for_change: I think I can do more and having more projects to work on would make me happy.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fears that pursuing a more fulfilling role might disrupt a stable, albeit unsatisfying, situation where the company depends on him.

values_and_stakes: His sense of identity as a proactive person who likes to stay busy and obtain goals.
His current job and the perceived dependence the company has on him.
(inferred) The stability and predictability of his current employment situation.
key_facts: Most days he only has 2 hours of work but is at his desk for 8 hours.
He has not yet talked to his work about additional projects.
He directly asked the therapist if asking for more work would be 'weird'.

background: (inferred) A woman in a long-term relationship since high school, currently unemployed or with unspecified occupation, lacking a strong social support network.
self_view_of_problem: She frames the problem as being stuck in a cycle where she invested years into a boyfriend who cheated repeatedly, then he broke up with her after she cheated once, leaving her feeling mad, alone, and like she wasted her life.
resistance_drivers: Expresses longing to return to the relationship when therapist questions its health, triggered by fear of being alone and losing her history.
Minimizes her own cheating by comparing it to his repeated infidelity, triggered when discussing accountability or fairness.

ambivalence.for_change: She admits the relationship lacked mutual respect and that she needs to learn from the past and stop repeating it.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) She fears losing her identity as someone's long-term partner and the dream of marrying her high school sweetheart, which feels like an irreplaceable life investment.

values_and_stakes: Her investment of years since high school, which she feels is wasted time she can't get back.
The potential future of marrying her high school sweetheart, a dream she's held despite his proposal never becoming official.
(inferred) Her social identity and validation, as she lacks friends and fears being alone without the relationship's drama and role.
key_facts: Her boyfriend cheated on her many times, while she cheated once before he broke up with her.
She has no friends to turn to and feels nobody wants to listen to her drama.
She immediately latches onto the therapist's suggestion of revenge through self-improvement and dating someone hot.

background: (inferred) A married man whose best friend since high school flirted with his wife and propositioned her for sex at a party.
self_view_of_problem: My best friend did an unacceptable thing that makes me disgusted and very angry; I want to smash his face.
resistance_drivers: Rejects non-violent emotional release when it conflicts with his immediate physical anger (e.g., dismisses crying, wants to hit something).
Deflects from practical solutions by refocusing on the anger and its social consequences (e.g., shifts from action steps to the impact on friend group).

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) He wants to avoid getting in trouble from physical violence and seeks a way to manage his anger.
ambivalence.against_change: He is attached to the cathartic release of physical violence as the rightful expression of his anger.

values_and_stakes: His long-term friendship since high school with the perpetrator.
His shared social circle and the stability of those common friendships.
His self-image as a man who responds decisively to a profound betrayal.
key_facts: He explicitly states he wants to smash his friend's face.
He does not go to the gym, so punching a bag is not an immediate option.
He plans to ring his friend to express his feelings directly.

background: A warehouse worker who started the job one month ago, currently living with the anxiety of an unreported workplace accident.
self_view_of_problem: I made an accident at work and didn't report it, and now I have fear and anxiety that if management finds out I will get in trouble and lose my job.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by seeking reassurance about logistical details (e.g., when to report) when pressured to take immediate action.
Engages in wishful thinking about the accident not being discovered (e.g., citing old cameras, large warehouse) to avoid the feared consequence of reporting.
(inferred) Minimizes personal agency by attributing outcomes to external luck ('the luck is not always on my side') rather than his own choices.

ambivalence.for_change: He regrets not reporting it and knows he did wrong, and it bothers him because he doesn't want to lose his job.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is pulled away from reporting by a deep fear of immediate job loss and shame, which feels more certain and punishing than the abstract value of honesty.

values_and_stakes: His current warehouse job, which he needs as he states it's very hard to find a job now.
(inferred) His standing and reputation as a reliable new employee in his team and with management.
(inferred) His self-concept as a competent and honest person, which is threatened by his own inaction.
key_facts: The accident happened two days ago, and he has not reported it.
He was told in training that delaying an accident report will result in losing the job for sure.
He plans to text the therapist tomorrow after work depending on how things go.

background: (inferred) The client works in a logistics or distribution role at a company where they have been employed for five years, responsible for coordinating lorry collections to fulfill customer orders.
self_view_of_problem: I made a mistake at work today and I have a fear that I will get in serious trouble, possibly losing my job, which causes me so much stress I can't breathe normally.
resistance_drivers: Minimizes the therapist's suggestions by expressing dislike or unfamiliarity (e.g., 'I just don't really like classic music but I can try').
Seeks repeated reassurance about job security despite therapist's attempts to redirect or reassure (e.g., repeatedly asking 'Do you think I will lose my job?').

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to reduce my overwhelming stress and fear about tomorrow's meeting, so I am willing to try new relaxation techniques like meditation.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) If I accept that my mistake is minor and manageable, I might lose the protective vigilance that I believe prevents future, potentially catastrophic, errors.

values_and_stakes: My job of five years, which provides financial security and stability.
My professional reputation and standing within my team, where 'before me nobody made a mistake such as this one'.
(inferred) My sense of competence and reliability as an employee, which is threatened by this error.
key_facts: The client's mistake resulted in one lorry not being collected, delaying orders for around 300 customers.
This is the client's first mistake of this kind in five years at the company.
The client has a meeting scheduled with their manager tomorrow to discuss the incident.

background: The client currently works a night job in a motel, where they have lived on-site, and has over 15 years of experience in a related field, plus additional customer service experience. They are seeking a new job for better pay and appreciation.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as a frustrating job search where employers do not acknowledge applications, and their current job does not pay what their skills are worth and leaves them feeling taken for granted.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from practical problem-solving by elaborating on the ideal job's benefits when the therapist suggests alternatives like relocation or checking vacancies.
Minimizes the difficulty of the job market by focusing on safety concerns and the scarcity of 'decent' jobs, avoiding broader search strategies.

ambivalence.for_change: The client strongly desires change, explicitly stating they would relocate 'in a heartbeat' for the dream job to gain better pay, appreciation, and a sense of ministry.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is an emotional attachment to their current stable, though unappreciated, routine and identity, making the uncertainty of a new job search daunting.

values_and_stakes: Their sense of religious calling and ministry, tied to working at a church-owned conference center.
Deep, familial relationships with colleagues and a community where they feel valued and connected.
Financial stability and fair compensation for their skills, which are currently at risk in their underpaying job.
key_facts: The client submitted an application for their dream job last week and has heard nothing back, indicating high anticipation and potential for disappointment.
They have over 15 years of directly related experience and strong references, including from their pastor and former trainer.
They currently work nights and have lived on-site at their motel job, showing adaptability to residential work environments.

background: (inferred) A university student facing academic pressure and potential failure due to procrastination and gaming.
self_view_of_problem: I fall behind on study because I played too much online games and didn't attend classes, and now I'm trying to catch up 3 months of study in one week.
resistance_drivers: Rejects simplistic reassurance (e.g., 'try to relax') as insufficient for the depth of his problem.
(inferred) Seeks external solutions (like medication) when internal coping feels inadequate, indicating a pattern of looking for quick fixes.

ambivalence.for_change: He wants to pass his exams and is sacrificing sleep (4 hours per night) to try to catch up.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is attached to the escapism and immediate gratification of online gaming, which conflicts with the sustained effort of studying.

values_and_stakes: His academic success and passing his university exams for the year.
(inferred) His self-image as a capable student, which is threatened by potential failure.
(inferred) His physical and mental health, which is being compromised by severe sleep deprivation.
key_facts: He is attempting to compress 3 months of missed study into one week.
He is currently sleeping only about 4 hours per day.
He has missed classes due to playing online games.

background: (inferred) A man in the process of divorce after his wife's infidelity with a friend; he works a job with an early morning shift.
self_view_of_problem: He defines the problem as having depression and feeling devastated due to his wife's betrayal and the divorce, and he feels his friends and colleagues are talking about him behind his back.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Shifts focus to practical obstacles (like lack of time or not knowing where to start) when given direct advice, avoiding deeper emotional engagement.
(inferred) Seeks external validation or new relationships (like dating) as a quick fix, rather than addressing the core emotional pain.

ambivalence.for_change: He admits he feels depressed, unfocused, and devastated, and wants the depression to go away.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) He is emotionally attached to his wife and the past relationship, stating he still loves her, which pulls him away from fully accepting the divorce and moving on.

values_and_stakes: His marriage and relationship with his wife, which is ending but he still loves her.
His social standing and reputation among his friends and colleagues, which he fears is being damaged by gossip.
(inferred) His sense of trust and loyalty, shattered by the betrayal of both his wife and his friend.
key_facts: He wakes up at 5 AM and his work shift starts at 6 AM, leaving him little personal time.
He reports he cannot sleep properly at night.
He feels unfocused at work and thinks about the betrayal and divorce constantly.

background: (inferred) A person recently unemployed, likely due to COVID-19 lockdowns, who is taking new courses to improve job prospects.
self_view_of_problem: I'm in depression because I lost my job, and it's a very difficult time due to the COVID lockdown and a difficult market situation.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from discussing concrete job search efforts by refocusing on external, uncontrollable factors like the market and crisis.
Expresses doubt about the efficacy of suggested actions (like taking courses) with passive 'let's see' statements, showing a lack of agency.

ambivalence.for_change: I'm taking new courses to get a new job, indicating a desire to improve my situation.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear that effort will be futile due to external circumstances, protecting against the disappointment of failure.

values_and_stakes: Financial security and professional identity tied to having a job.
(inferred) Self-worth and sense of competence, which are threatened by prolonged unemployment.
key_facts: The client lost their job recently, which is the direct cause of their stated depression.
The client is currently taking new courses but expresses uncertainty about whether they will help.
The client repeatedly emphasizes the difficult market and COVID crisis as barriers.

background: A college student majoring in public health, living with an older sister who is an essential worker, and planning to apply to graduate school next year.
self_view_of_problem: I have anxiety as a college student learning during the pandemic, with difficulty staying focused in classes due to distance learning, anxiety, and loneliness, which has caused my grades to suffer a little, and I lack motivation to get started on grad school applications.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by turning questions back to the therapist when asked about personal problems (e.g., asking the therapist for tips on handling anxiety instead of exploring their own).
Minimizes their own struggles by generalizing them ('times are tough right now for everyone') when suggestions are made.
(inferred) Avoids deeper emotional exploration by focusing on practical tasks (e.g., asking for tips on personal statements) when anxiety surfaces.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to overcome my anxiety and lack of motivation so I can successfully apply to grad school and pursue a career in public health.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Addressing my anxiety and isolation would require confronting difficult emotions and reaching out for support, which feels overwhelming and risky.

values_and_stakes: Academic success and strong grad school applications, which are at risk due to suffered grades and lack of focus.
The relationship with my older sister, which I protect by not troubling her with my problems.
(inferred) A sense of independence and self-reliance, which would be challenged by admitting need for help or connection.
key_facts: My grades suffered a little due to difficulty staying focused with distance learning.
I live with my older sister who is an essential worker and I don't want to trouble her.
I am applying to public health graduate programs next year.

background: (inferred) The client works in a medical office as part of an all-female staff, with a doctor as the boss and two office managers.
self_view_of_problem: I am worried my boss will judge me or fire me because I was the most drunk at a staff appreciation event, and I feel embarrassed and unsure how to redeem myself.
resistance_drivers: Prefers avoidance and letting the issue fade rather than directly addressing it, especially when feeling embarrassed.
Uses uncertainty about the boss's full knowledge of the event as a reason to avoid taking action, fearing that apologizing might reveal more than the boss knows.
(inferred) Defers to the group's reaction (coworkers laughing it off) to justify inaction, despite sensing the boss's changed perception.

ambivalence.for_change: I know I should probably apologize to seem professional and get into my boss's good grace, and I will eventually do the right thing.
ambivalence.against_change: I feel a strong pull to avoid the discomfort and potential embarrassment of a direct conversation, hoping the problem will just fade away on its own.

values_and_stakes: My professional reputation and standing with my boss, which affects my job security.
My sense of dignity and avoidance of further embarrassment in front of my coworkers and boss.
(inferred) The cohesive, informal dynamic of the all-female office staff, which might be altered by formal apologies or HR involvement.
key_facts: The client was the most drunk person at the staff event, and a coworker was injured and taken to the ER.
The boss left after the injury, so his full knowledge of how drunk everyone got is uncertain.
The client has 10 years of work experience and has never encountered a situation like this before.

background: The client is raising their grandchild and has a medical condition (a medication causing low white blood cell count) that limits their ability to go out, especially during COVID. (inferred) They are an avid reader.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as being lonely because friends and family only seek them out when they need a problem solved, not to listen or have a light conversation. They feel their attempts to speak up about this go nowhere.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from concrete action by citing external barriers (health, COVID) when the therapist suggests going out to meet people.
Seeks therapist validation and agreement ('Do you understand what I mean?') before exploring their own feelings or solutions more deeply.
(inferred) Minimizes their own emotional needs by stating 'I’m honestly not that needy' while expressing significant distress about not being heard.

ambivalence.for_change: They feel excited about the idea of joining online groups to find people with similar interests and support.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) They are attached to their current relationships and fears losing their valued role as a reliable problem-solver, even though it leaves them feeling used.

values_and_stakes: Their established role as the reliable problem-solver within their current family and friend network.
The practical and emotional support system provided by their current friends and family, however limited.
(inferred) Their identity as a capable caregiver and grandparent, which might feel threatened by shifting focus to their own social needs.
key_facts: The client is raising their grandchild, which limits their time and social flexibility.
A medication side effect (low white blood cell count) combined with COVID significantly restricts their ability to go out in public.
A friend previously told the client they were 'blowing it out of proportion' when they expressed their feelings.

background: (inferred) A working adult with a family, living in a new city where they have few social connections. They rely on their car for work and have exhausted savings during the pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is a compounding financial burden caused by unexpected car trouble and a mechanic bill that is growing, exacerbated by the loss of their wife's income.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Minimizes or deflects when discussing external assistance (e.g., food banks) due to a sense of pride or comparative hardship.
(inferred) Focuses on immediate, concrete obstacles (like a bill) rather than systemic or emotional patterns.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) A desire to alleviate the immediate financial pressure and secure stability for their family.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) An emotional pull away from accepting help due to pride, self-sufficiency, and a belief that others are more deserving.

values_and_stakes: Financial independence and the ability to pay bills without external aid.
The family's stability, including caring for their three-year-old child.
The wife's employment and contribution to household income.
key_facts: The client's car is essential for work and its repair bill is escalating.
The wife has lost her job and is seeking new work, with interviews scheduled.
The family has used up all savings during the pandemic and moved to a new city, limiting social support.

background: (inferred) A person who shops at second-hand stores, has a disorganized wardrobe with many baggy clothes, and attends regular virtual counseling sessions.
self_view_of_problem: People make fun of my appearance because I don't have fancy clothes and my clothes don't look good on me; it's hard to feel so different.
resistance_drivers: Deflects practical suggestions by citing external barriers (e.g., COVID, lack of money) to avoid taking action.
Seeks external validation for a shift in perspective (e.g., asking 'So I should not care so much what they say about me?') rather than generating it internally.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to get better at picking clothes that make me happy and learn to alter my clothes to fit better.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear that changing my appearance or caring less about others' opinions might not stop the bullying or make me feel accepted.

values_and_stakes: Financial security — not having a lot of money to buy new clothes.
Personal comfort and safety — avoiding confrontation due to COVID and a preference for baggy clothes.
The therapeutic relationship — valuing connection with someone who has shared similar experiences.
key_facts: The client receives compliments when wearing clothes that fit nicely.
The client loves second-hand stores.
The client has a lot of clothes that don't look good on her.

background: (inferred) A young adult or adolescent living at home, likely a student or unemployed, spending most of their time isolated in their room playing video games.
self_view_of_problem: I'm just lazy on everything and don't have any motivation anymore; I don't have the courage or guts to seek help because I'm really shy.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from professional help by shifting focus to maintaining limited social contact through gaming.
Uses minimization ('just lazy') to avoid labeling the problem as depression requiring external intervention.

ambivalence.for_change: I know I should seek help and set aside my pride, hoping to muster the courage.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Fear of exposing vulnerability and shame to a stranger, tied to shyness and pride.

values_and_stakes: Connection with friends through voice calls and gaming — a remaining social lifeline.
(inferred) Self-image as someone who is independent and not needing help, tied to pride.
(inferred) The safety and predictability of isolation in their room, a controlled environment.
key_facts: Client has stopped talking to their family.
Client's lack of motivation predates the pandemic.
Client only socializes through voice calls while playing games.

background: A recent college graduate living in a different country from their parents, currently considering pursuing a master's degree but uncertain about a doctorate. (inferred) They have a history of therapy and lost a job during COVID, receiving financial support from parents.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as being forced by parents into a major they don't enjoy, leading to uncertainty about continuing education and a fear of failure, compounded by a lifelong pattern of parental pressure that makes it 'really hard to make decisions on my own now.'
resistance_drivers: Deflects from exploring independent desires by returning to the theme of parental pressure and obligation.
Minimizes their own agency and preferences by stating 'I don't really know anymore what I actually like.'
(inferred) Avoids directly confronting the therapist's suggestions about financial independence or the father's own regrets, shifting focus back to parental expectations.

ambivalence.for_change: They feel a point where they 'couldn't function anymore' and sought therapy, indicating a pull toward relief from distress and autonomy.
ambivalence.against_change: A deep-seated fear of disappointing their parents and losing their approval, tied to a family identity where they are the 'perfect individual' carrying collective hopes.

values_and_stakes: The approval and emotional connection with their parents, maintained through regular Skype calls and a sense of obligation.
Their role as the family's successful 'perfect individual,' fulfilling academic and musical ambitions their father could not.
(inferred) The financial safety net and support from parents, especially highlighted after job loss during COVID.
key_facts: The client had a therapy conversation with their parents two months ago that initially seemed successful but then reverted to old patterns.
The client lives in a different country from their parents but maintains regular contact via Skype.
The client lost their job during COVID and accepted financial help from their parents.

background: (inferred) A person who recently ended a six-month romantic relationship and is experiencing significant disruption to their daily life.
self_view_of_problem: I am very depressed due to the breakup and cannot go on with my daily life.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Withholds or has not initiated actions they acknowledge could help, like talking to close friends.
(inferred) Expresses a lack of existing hobbies or structured activities to engage with.

ambivalence.for_change: They are willing to try suggestions like talking to friends and planning travel to feel better.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) A fear that moving on means letting go of the past relationship and its associated identity.

values_and_stakes: The daily life routine and functionality they have lost.
(inferred) The emotional security and identity tied to the past six-month relationship.
(inferred) The potential comfort and predictability of their current depressed state versus the uncertainty of change.
key_facts: The client broke up with their partner of six months.
The client has a couple of close friends but has not talked to them about the breakup.
The client states they do not have any hobby per se but would like to travel to new places.

background: A recovering alcoholic with 52 days of sobriety, diagnosed with inattentive ADHD and an underlying heart condition that prevents standard medication. (inferred) Has a therapist and is on a 10-week post-detox intensive plan with a good support network.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is that my mental health (inattentive ADHD) cannot be properly medicated because of my heart condition, causing low mood and struggle, and I used alcohol as self-medication which I miss.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from exploring emotional pain by shifting focus to medical limitations (e.g., heart condition preventing medication).
Uses politeness and gratitude to maintain distance and avoid deeper vulnerability (e.g., thanking therapist for time, saying 'I have plenty but im sure we dont have the time').

ambivalence.for_change: I want to live outside my own sideways mind and not be frustrated and angry with myself, believing I have so much to offer society if I can rectify this.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I am attached to the identity of someone who is medically limited and destined to be absent-minded, which provides a stable, if painful, explanation for my struggles.

values_and_stakes: My sobriety and the 52-day recovery progress are at risk if I cannot find an alternative to alcohol for managing ADHD symptoms.
My potential to contribute to society and offer something valuable is at risk if I remain stuck in my current mental state.
(inferred) My current support network and therapeutic plan stability are at risk if I become too frustrated and angry with myself, potentially leading to disengagement.
key_facts: The client has 52 days of sobriety from alcohol, which was used as self-medication for ADHD symptoms.
The client has an underlying heart condition that prevents the use of recommended ADHD medication.
The client is currently on a 10-week post-detox intensive plan and has a therapist and good support network.

background: (inferred) A student currently enrolled in a semester of school, experiencing significant academic pressure.
self_view_of_problem: I am having too much anxiety due to pressure from the studies and don't know how to deal with it.
resistance_drivers: Rejects practical suggestions that involve altering the academic structure (like taking time off or dropping a class) by stating they are not an option.
Expresses skepticism about the applicability of solutions (like a sick note) by questioning if they qualify or if it would hurt their grade.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want relief from the anxiety and pressure that is making me unable to cope.
ambivalence.against_change: I am attached to maintaining my current academic trajectory and grade integrity without appearing 'sick' or needing special accommodation.

values_and_stakes: My academic performance and grades.
My identity as a competent student who is not 'sick'.
(inferred) My progression through the semester without delay or disruption.
key_facts: The client is in the middle of a semester and feels trapped by the pressure.
The client has an elder sister they feel they can talk to.
The client agreed to try to make an appointment with a counselor next week.

background: (inferred) A person who recently ended a two-year romantic relationship and is currently experiencing significant emotional distress.
self_view_of_problem: I am extremely depressed after the breakup, which happened suddenly, and I don't know how to get out of it.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Withdraws into isolation when feeling depressed, rejecting social support.
(inferred) Shows passive agreement with suggestions rather than active engagement in problem-solving.

ambivalence.for_change: I feel better talking to you, indicating a desire for relief and connection.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The depression provides a familiar emotional state that protects from the immediate pain of the sudden loss.

values_and_stakes: The two-year romantic relationship that has ended.
(inferred) The identity and daily life structure built around being in that partnership.
(inferred) The ability to engage in previously enjoyed activities like playing the flute.
key_facts: The client was in a two-year relationship that ended recently and suddenly.
The client states they have no one they can share their feelings with.
The client plays the flute and is considering picking it up again.

background: I'm a therapist experiencing burnout in my profession, and I have my own therapist who I suspect is also burnt out.
self_view_of_problem: I'm in limbo — my job feels like a gray slog every day, and I'm burning out, but I feel obligated to my patients and uncertain about making a change.
resistance_drivers: Deflects with humor or hypotheticals when faced with direct suggestions for change (e.g., joking about computers replacing therapists).
Expresses uncertainty and 'I don't know' statements when concrete steps (like retraining, time off, or medication) are proposed.
Uses obligation to patients as a reason to avoid actions that would prioritize self-care (e.g., taking time off or reducing workload).

ambivalence.for_change: I want to be responsible to myself and feel better, and I've thought about traveling or reducing my workload.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I fear that changing my professional role or taking medication might threaten my identity as a competent, committed therapist and disrupt the stability I have.

values_and_stakes: My professional commitment and relationship with my patients — they might question my dedication if I take time off.
My identity and effectiveness as a therapist — I worry medication could impair my job performance.
The stability and familiarity of my current career path, despite its burnout, versus the uncertainty of retraining or major change.
key_facts: I have already considered lightening my workload or going part-time as a potential step.
I have a therapist who has recommended medication, which I am hesitant about.
I feel that my hobbies are less fun because my job is less fun, indicating a spillover effect.

background: (inferred) A person experiencing social isolation, likely living alone or with limited social contact, with friends who are currently unavailable.
self_view_of_problem: My friends won't hang out with me, and I am alone all the time; I am a loner.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Deflects from exploring the social problem by quickly accepting and shifting focus to generic self-improvement tasks when the therapist offers a personal example.
(inferred) Avoids setting specific, actionable goals for change when prompted, opting for vague intentions.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to hang out with people.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) An emotional attachment to the identity of 'a loner,' which provides a stable, if painful, self-concept that avoids the risk of rejection or failed social efforts.

values_and_stakes: (inferred) The stable, predictable identity of being 'a loner,' which, though painful, avoids the uncertainty and potential failure of trying to connect.
(inferred) The current passive relationship dynamic with friends, where the client is not the one initiating or risking rejection.
key_facts: The client explicitly states 'My friends won't hang out with me' and 'I am alone all the time.'
The client identifies themself as 'a loner' in response to the therapist's reflection.

When the therapist shares a personal coping strategy, the client immediately agrees with the suggestions ('That all sounds great') and proposes only vague implementation goals ('just start doing them and continue doing them').

background: (inferred) A person who was in a four-year relationship that recently ended when their partner left them for a wealthy man and is now engaged.
self_view_of_problem: My love is broken up, she left me alone, and I don't have any idea what to do.
resistance_drivers: Rejects advice to move on by citing the length and depth of the relationship ('but how could I, we are in a relationship for 4 years').
Counters suggestions for social support by stating friends mock him and family is not an easy option.
(inferred) Demonstrates passive compliance ('I will try') without genuine engagement, indicating a surface-level agreement to end the conversation.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) He wants to stop the painful, repeating memories that make him mad.
ambivalence.against_change: He is emotionally attached to the past relationship and its memories, which feel impossible to forget.

values_and_stakes: The four-year relationship and the identity built within it.
Social support from friends, which feels unavailable due to mockery.
(inferred) A sense of control and competence in managing his own emotional life.
key_facts: His partner left him for a rich man and is preparing to get married soon.
When he tries to forget her, memories repeat and sometimes make him mad.
His friends make fun of him when he shares his feelings.

background: (inferred) A person grieving the loss of a close friend who died a few years ago in a car accident, with a supportive family and social network.
self_view_of_problem: My friend died and it's so difficult for me; I know time is the only way to move on, however it's so difficult for me.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Deflects from deeper emotional exploration by shifting focus to practical solutions when asked about what could help.
(inferred) Minimizes the depth of their own grief by generalizing it ('It's so hard for anyone') when describing the loss.

ambivalence.for_change: I try going out with my family and friend, avoiding things that we used to do together, trying little by little.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The grief and sadness feel like a necessary, enduring connection to the lost friend, making moving on feel like a betrayal of that bond.

values_and_stakes: The memory and unique bond with her friend, who was like a sister and always took care of her.
(inferred) The stability and comfort of her current coping routine (avoiding shared activities, staying busy).
The supportive relationships with family and other friends that provide her current network.
key_facts: Her friend died suddenly in a car accident a few years ago, and the anniversary has stirred up the sadness.
She actively avoids things she used to do with her friend to manage her grief.
She plans to fill her schedule with activities like exercise, watching movies, and playing games to keep her mind occupied.

background: (inferred) An individual who was recently laid off after six years and four months at a job, likely living alone or with limited social support.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as 'the worst situation i met in this year' and 'my worst time,' caused by being laid off to reduce company expenses, which 'really shatters me.'
resistance_drivers: Redirects focus to the therapist's problems when the therapist shares a vulnerability ('dont think like that, it is very hard in that situation').
Acquiesces to suggestions without elaboration or follow-through, indicating passive compliance rather than active engagement ('i see, i will try to apply for it').

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) A desire to feel less shattered and isolated, and to secure a new job ('i would like to get any othe job').
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) An emotional pull toward maintaining a self-image as a competent, long-term employee who was unfairly laid off, which conflicts with actively seeking help or admitting need.

values_and_stakes: The respect and support of people around them, which is currently at risk because 'people aroud me are angry because i lost my job'.
(inferred) Their identity and self-worth tied to being a reliable, long-term employee at their former job.
(inferred) Financial stability and independence, threatened by the job loss and lack of immediate income.
key_facts: The client lost their job last week after working there for six years and four months.
The client has not applied for unemployment benefits.
The client reports that people around them are angry about the job loss and are not providing information or support when asked.

background: A man who was laid off from work in June of last year (mid-Covid-19 period). He is married with young children and relies on his wife's meagre earnings for financial support. (inferred) He is the primary male breadwinner in a family accustomed to spending on out-of-home activities.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as a financial crisis that started with an unexpected layoff, leading to an inability to meet family needs and fulfill his role as a provider, which in turn causes him significant anxiety and a feeling of letting his family down.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Expresses skepticism about the simplicity of suggested solutions (e.g., deep breaths, playing with kids) compared to the magnitude of his financial and role-based problems.
(inferred) Re-focuses conversation from emotional coping back to concrete financial lack and unmet family expectations when reassurance is offered.

ambivalence.for_change: He expresses a desire to manage his anxiety and 'adjust my attitude first and accept the situation,' showing a pull toward coping and hope.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) An emotional attachment to his identity as the primary provider and a fear that accepting the situation means failing his family, which pulls him away from change.

values_and_stakes: His role and identity as a man and primary provider for his family.
The specific joy and family bonding derived from out-of-home activities that require spending.
His children's expectations and happiness, as they are too young to understand the financial constraints but ask him to do things that cost money.
key_facts: He was laid off in June of last year at a time when he was already financially down.
His wife provides the only current income, which he describes as 'meagre earnings'.
His children are young and keep asking him to do things for them that require money, which he cannot do.

background: (inferred) The client is a man with a stable living situation and friends, but no explicit occupation or family details are provided.
self_view_of_problem: I feel really sad all the time and my life is not going in the right direction, but I can't find a reason because my health is fine and I have friends and a place to live.
resistance_drivers: Dismisses potential solutions based on gender stereotypes or cost concerns (e.g., 'I thought it was for women,' 'Is yoga expensive?').
Expresses skepticism that positive actions will produce lasting change (e.g., 'I feel ok when I'm with them, but then later, I feel sad again,' 'I'm trying to be positive. It doesn't seem to work.').

ambivalence.for_change: I really need some guidance here and want to know how to change my mood.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Feels a sense of helplessness and identity threat at the idea that change requires methods he perceives as unfamiliar or not fitting his self-image as a 'regular guy'.

values_and_stakes: His self-image as a 'regular guy' who doesn't use 'special clothes or equipment' like incense or candles.
His financial stability, as he mentions not having much money.
(inferred) His independence and not wanting to rely on others, as he hesitates about needing someone to help him learn meditation.
key_facts: He has tried meeting with friends but the positive effect is temporary.
He has not tried yoga, meditation, or therapy before.
He is willing to check out YouTube for meditation guidance after receiving reassurance about cost and simplicity.

background: (inferred) A person who is a close friend to someone who has lost a son, likely an adult with a significant personal relationship outside of family.
self_view_of_problem: The problem is how to deal with the terrible, unexpected loss of my best friend's son and my feeling of helplessness because there is nothing I can do to make her feel better.
resistance_drivers: Expresses helplessness and impossibility when the therapist suggests a path forward, framing the situation as unsolvable.
Deflects from their own grief by focusing exclusively on their friend's state, minimizing their own emotional needs.

ambivalence.for_change: I want to feel better and find a way to be helpful to my grieving friend.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is a pull to remain in a state of shared, inconsolable grief as a form of loyalty and connection to my friend.

values_and_stakes: The concrete relationship with my best friend, which could be strained if I fail to support her correctly.
(inferred) My role as a reliable, supportive companion in her time of need.
key_facts: The client's best friend's son died at age 26 after an accident on February 25th and holding on until February 28th.
The client feels helpless because they believe nothing they do can make their friend feel better.
The client accepted the therapy session/survey today and reports feeling a little better after the conversation.

background: A third-year college student majoring in computer engineering, whose parents are involved in their academic and financial decisions.
self_view_of_problem: School is going badly because the major is too hard and others are smarter, and it feels too late to switch due to time and money constraints.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from internal doubts by externalizing the problem onto perceived intellectual inferiority and parental pressure.
Uses practical constraints (time, money) as a barrier to avoid committing to a decision about changing paths.

ambivalence.for_change: Admits not wanting to be a computer engineer and would switch majors in a heartbeat if money and time weren't concerns.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) Feels attached to the security and approval of staying on the current, expected path to avoid disappointing parents or facing financial uncertainty.

values_and_stakes: Parental financial support and approval, which could be jeopardized by extending college or changing majors.
Time investment already made in the computer engineering degree, which would be lost if switching.
(inferred) The stable career identity and future job prospects associated with the current major.
key_facts: The client is at the end of their third year in computer engineering.
The client has already spoken to a school counselor about options.
The client is considering a joint Zoom meeting with parents and a counselor.

background: He worked in IT for 14 years and recently lost his job, which puts his home and family at risk.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as a loss of his job leading to a dire situation where he might lose his home and family, and a loss of his confidence, self-worth, and self-esteem.
resistance_drivers: Deflects with polite agreement ('thanks for the advice') when the therapist offers optimistic suggestions, rather than engaging with the substance.
(inferred) Minimizes his own prospects by citing external barriers ('companies want the newer younger versions') when his competence is affirmed.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) He feels a pull to 'get straight back in the game' to secure his home and family.
ambivalence.against_change: He feels a pull away from change because seeking a new job threatens his identity and self-worth by forcing him to start over as an older worker in a field that values youth.

values_and_stakes: His home, which he is at risk of losing.
His family stability, which is threatened by the financial situation.
His professional identity built over 14 years in IT, which is challenged by starting over.
key_facts: He lost his IT job after 14 years of work.
He rates his odds of finding a new job at only 60%.
He believes companies prefer 'newer younger versions' of workers.

background: (inferred) The client is employed and works at the same place as a friend, which complicates their social situation.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as being disgusted by a friend's immoral cheating and questioning whether to remain friends, while also feeling it's not their business and wanting to avoid confrontation.
resistance_drivers: Deflects from direct action by minimizing the problem as 'not my business' when the therapist suggests addressing it.
Prefers passive avoidance (e.g., ghosting, ignoring) over direct communication when the therapist proposes assertive steps.

ambivalence.for_change: The client feels disgust and questions the friendship, indicating a pull toward distancing themselves from someone they see as immoral.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) The client fears the social and practical complications of a confrontation or ending the friendship, especially due to their shared workplace.

values_and_stakes: A valued friendship is at risk if they distance themselves.
Workplace harmony and daily comfort are at risk if they create tension with a colleague.
(inferred) Their self-image as a non-confrontational person who avoids drama is at risk if they take direct action.
key_facts: The client's friend cheated on her boyfriend, who is described as a nice guy and is unaware.
The client and the friend work at the same place, making avoidance logistically difficult.
The client has already tried to create distance, but the friend continues to initiate contact.

background: The client is employed in a role where they are the only person doing their specific job, and they have a boyfriend who encourages them to set boundaries. (inferred) They are experiencing high work stress and long hours during the pandemic.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as an overwhelming workload they cannot keep up with, causing stress and anxiety, and feels their manager and company do not understand or help.
resistance_drivers: Deflects by externalizing blame onto management's unwillingness to hire or listen, avoiding personal agency.
Minimizes personal power and frames self as powerless to change the situation when challenged.
Avoids assertive action for fear of social repercussions, like being seen as a complainer by coworkers.

ambivalence.for_change: They admit feeling that something needs to happen and it might be time to take a risk to gain control.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) They are attached to avoiding conflict and maintaining a positive, non-complaining social identity at work.

values_and_stakes: Their current job and financial stability during a pandemic with limited other opportunities.
Their relationships with coworkers and desire to not be seen as annoying or a constant complainer.
Their relationship with their boyfriend, who advocates for boundaries they struggle to implement.
key_facts: The client has been working 14-hour days all week.
The client has tried talking to their line manager, who does not seem to understand how busy they are.
The client is keeping an eye out for other jobs but perceives limited opportunities due to the pandemic.

background: A man with a wife and children, currently quarantined alone at home after testing positive for Covid-19. (inferred) He has high blood pressure and is on the older side but not a senior citizen.
self_view_of_problem: He frames it as a frustrating and unlucky timing failure: 'I feel like a couple more months or so and I'd have the vaccine. Made it a year, then get infected during the stretch run of this pandemic.'
resistance_drivers: Rejects overly positive reframing of his situation, correcting the therapist's metaphor with his own (e.g., 'I was fighting it, but Covid won this week!', 'I'm only in like the third inning or so right now though').
Expresses pessimism about long-term solutions when the therapist offers hopeful generalities (e.g., responding to hope for a permanent solution with 'I don't know if that will ever happen').

ambivalence.for_change: He wants to recover quickly and return to his family, as shown by his focus on the quarantine countdown: '10 days cannot come fast enough.'
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) There is a pull toward accepting a narrative of defeat or bad luck, which protects him from the frustration of having fought precautions for a year only to get sick just before vaccination.

values_and_stakes: His immediate physical presence and role with his family, as they have left the home during his quarantine.
His health and safety, given his age and pre-existing high blood pressure which raises his medical risk.
His sense of personal victory and resilience, which is threatened by contracting the virus after a year of avoidance.
key_facts: He tested positive for Covid-19 on Wednesday and is in a 10-day quarantine away from his family.
He has mild cold-like symptoms (body aches, stuffy head, sore throat) but no severe symptoms currently.
He was approximately a couple of months away from being eligible for the Covid-19 vaccine when he became infected.

background: (inferred) The client is employed in a workplace where they have a co-worker who is being harassed by their boss, and they are concerned about the situation.
self_view_of_problem: The client frames the problem as 'my boss keeps hitting on a co-worker, who really doesn't like the guy' and is asking 'What can I do to make it stop?'
